scope: Published component modules and Storybook composition recipes. Theme providers are documented separately on the Theme page.
evidence: Source-derived inventory and documented contracts; not a claim of executed interaction, visual or assistive-technology tests.

components.title: Accordion
components.purpose: `Accordion` stacks sections that open and close under their titles. It suits content people scan for the one part they need (frequently asked questions, detail most people skip, sections of a review page), so the page stays short.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The WAI-ARIA accordion pattern: each title is a `button` inside a heading, with
  `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`; each open section is a `region` labelled by
  its title.
- Set `headingLevel` so the titles fit the page's heading outline (3 by default).
- Tab moves through the titles and into open content. Arrow keys also move
  between titles, Home and End to the ends; Enter or Space toggles.
- Opening and closing animate the height, and don't animate when people ask for
  reduced motion.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't put required form fields in a closed section.** People miss them,
  and errors inside closed sections are invisible.
- **Don't nest accordions.**
- **Don't make titles vague.** "More information" five times tells people nothing;
  each title should say what is inside.

components.title: Alert
components.purpose: `Alert` surfaces a status message tied to a recent action or system state. Use it for in-flow messaging that the reader should see but that doesn't need to interrupt them. For modal interruptions use a Dialog; for transient feedback prefer a Toast.
documentationSections: A theme's own colours as tones

guidance.Accessibility:
- `error` and `warning` render with `role="alert"` so assistive tech announces them immediately.
- `info` and `success` use `role="status"` — announced politely, without interrupting the screen-reader queue. So does a tone from a colour the theme added.
- `variant` changes only the edge and border; the role and text contrast are the same.
- The dismiss button carries `aria-label="Dismiss"` and a visible focus ring (`theme.colors.border.focus`).
- The Alert scopes default content foreground roles against its tone background. Code and Kbd keep their own surfaces and calculate their own contrast; no tag-wide CSS override forces their text to inherit the Alert foreground. Verify explicit semantic tones and custom color overrides in their actual composition.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use `error` for non-actionable messages.** It triggers an immediate screen-reader interruption; reserve it for things the user must address.
- **Don't pile up identical alerts.** Coalesce repeats ("12 tests broke") rather than rendering 12 alerts in a row.
- **Don't put critical actions inside an alert without a fallback elsewhere.** If the user dismisses, the action must remain reachable.

components.title: AreaChart
components.purpose: `AreaChart` shows a volume over an ordered axis, usually time: sightings logged per week, dues collected per month. It is a line with a light wash of the series colour beneath it, so the space under the line reads as "how much". Stacked, the top edge is the total and each band is one part of it. For rates, percentages and prices, where the area under the line means nothing, use a [LineChart](?path=/docs/functional-line-chart--docs). To compare parts across unordered categories, use a stacked [BarChart](?path=/docs/functional-bar-chart--docs); for one moment's split of a whole, a [DonutChart](?path=/docs/functional-donut-chart--docs).

guidance.Accessibility:
- The chart is a `<figure>` named by `title` and described by `description`. `title` is required; `hideTitle` hides it visually only.
- The "Table view" toggle button (`aria-pressed`) swaps the plot for a table of every value, captioned with `title`. It is the dependable way to read exact values with a keyboard, screen reader or magnifier.
- The plot is focusable (`role="application"`); arrow keys step through the points and show each point's tooltip.
- Colour never works alone: two or more series get a legend, the tooltip names each series, and the table labels each column. Light-mode slots 3 to 5 are under 3:1 contrast on white, which is why the legend and table view are always present.
- Text never takes a series colour. Name series in words rather than colouring a caption to match its band.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Stacking things that don't add up.** If the total is meaningless, the top edge lies. Leave `stacked` off, or use a LineChart.
- **An area chart for a rate.** Interest rates and percentages have no "volume"; the wash suggests one. Use a LineChart.
- **Many overlapping unstacked series.** Washes muddy each other past two. Stack them if they add up, otherwise use a LineChart or small multiples.
- **Two value axes.** There is no dual-axis option. Put measures with different units in separate charts.
- **More than eight series.** Only the first eight are drawn. Fold the small ones into "Other".
- **A rainbow stack.** Eight thin bands read as noise. Keep the stack to the three or four parts people compare and fold the rest.
- **Raising `--chart-area-opacity` to make it "pop".** A solid fill hides the lines and gridlines behind it.

components.title: Avatar
components.purpose: `Avatar` represents a person — preferring a photo when available, falling back to initials when not. The fallback background is hashed from `name` so the same user gets the same color across sessions and surfaces. Sizing is driven by the surrounding `Presentation` register, not a prop, so a stack of avatars stays in scale with its parent.

guidance.Accessibility: - The wrapper carries `role="img"` and `aria-label={name}`, so the user is always identified — image or initials. - The inner `` uses empty `alt=""` to prevent screen readers from announcing the same name twice. - The deterministic background color always meets contrast with the computed text color via `getMinContrastTextColor` — pastel hashes don't break legibility. - A native `title` attribute provides a hover tooltip for sighted users.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't pass a size prop — there isn't one.** To scale, wrap in a `Presentation` register; that way nested controls (buttons, badges) scale together.
- **Don't use `circle` for non-human entities.** Bots, services, and workspaces should be `rounded` so the shape carries meaning.
- **Don't rely on the hashed color as a brand color.** It's deterministic but not curated — fine for differentiation, not for marketing surfaces.
- **Don't omit `name`.** It's the alt text, the tooltip, and the seed for initials and color — without it the avatar is meaningless to assistive tech.

components.title: Badge
components.purpose: `Badge` reports the state or count of the thing beside it: "Overdue", "Paid", "3". The system sets it and it changes on its own; people never act on it. Use the `tone` for *meaning* (success, warning, error) and the `variant` for *emphasis* (`subtle` for ambient state, `solid` for headline status, `outline` for a quieter callout). A value people chose or can remove is a `Tag`; a flow-level message is an `Alert`.
documentationSections: A theme's own colours as tones

guidance.Accessibility:
- Tone is conveyed by color *and* text — never use a tone alone to signal state. The `dot` variant always keeps its text; the dot itself is `aria-hidden`.
- A colour the theme added gets the same contrast-checked palette as a built-in tone, but check your own colours in light and dark mode.
- Reduced-motion users see a static status dot.
- The pulsing dot carries `aria-hidden="true"`; the meaning lives in the label text.
- `solid` and `subtle` variants are checked via `getMinContrastTextColor` / `themeHelpers.darken` to hit WCAG AA on every tone.
- When used as a link or button (`as="a" / as="button"`), the underlying element supplies the focus ring and keyboard semantics.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use `dot` for the one status that matters.** A dot is quiet on purpose. The status of the record a page is about is a `subtle` or `solid` pill.
- **Don't pulse a badge that isn't actually live.** If the data is from a 5-minute-old poll, the breathing dot lies. Use `subtle` instead.
- **Don't pair `solid` with long copy.** Solid badges scream — reserve them for one or two words.
- **Don't make a Badge interactive.** Badges report; they never link, toggle or remove. Something people pick or remove is a `Tag`; a count on an action sits inside the `Button`.
- **Don't use a Badge for a value or category.** "Waikato Chapter" as a chosen filter, or a record's category, is a `Tag`.
- **Don't use Badge for flow-level messages.** A failed build summary belongs in an `Alert`, not a badge.

components.title: BarChart
components.purpose: `BarChart` compares magnitudes across categories: dues invoiced by quarter, sightings logged by chapter, sightings under review by sighting type. Bars grow from one baseline at zero, so their lengths compare honestly; hover, or (for vertical bars) focus the plot and use the arrow keys, to read each value, and the "Table view" toggle lists them all. For a continuous trend over many points in time, a [LineChart](?path=/docs/functional-line-chart--docs) reads better; for two to five parts of one whole where the share is the point, a [DonutChart](?path=/docs/functional-donut-chart--docs); for a single value against a range, a [Meter](?path=/docs/functional-meter--docs).

guidance.Accessibility:
- The chart is a `<figure>` named by `title` and described by `description`. `title` is required; `hideTitle` hides it visually only.
- The "Table view" toggle button (`aria-pressed`) swaps the plot for a table of every value, captioned with `title`: the dependable way to read exact values with a keyboard, screen reader or magnifier.
- With vertical bars the plot is focusable (`role="application"`); focus shows the first category and the left and right arrow keys step through the rest. With `orientation="horizontal"` the plot isn't a focus stop, because the arrow keys can't step through it; keyboard users read the values from the table view.
- Colour never works alone: two or more series get a legend, the tooltip names each series, and the table labels each column. Light-mode slots 3 to 5 are under 3:1 contrast on white, which is why the legend and table view are always present.
- Text never takes a series colour; legend labels, ticks and tooltip values stay in text colours.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **A cut value axis.** Bars always start at zero; don't try to "zoom in" by offsetting data. If the differences are small, show the change itself (as in the negative-values example) or use a LineChart.
- **Two value axes.** There is no dual-axis option. Chart dollars and counts separately.
- **A colour per category.** A rainbow of bars adds a legend's worth of decoding for nothing; the axis names each bar. Use one series colour and let length do the work.
- **More than eight series.** Only the first eight are drawn. Fold the small ones into "Other", or use small multiples.
- **Vertical columns with long names.** Labels collide or get skipped. Switch to `orientation="horizontal"`.
- **Unsorted rankings.** A ranked horizontal chart is read top-down; sort the rows largest first.
- **Stacking parts that don't add up.** The bar's length becomes a meaningless total. Group them instead.
- **A pie of many parts drawn as a donut.** Past five parts, a sorted horizontal BarChart compares them far better.

components.title: Block
components.purpose: `Block` is the universal styling primitive — a polymorphic `<div>` with theme-driven props for padding, background, radius, width, and border. Reach for it when you need a styled wrapper that doesn't earn its own named `Layout` component — the "give me a themed div" escape hatch that keeps consumer code free of `styled-components`. It does **not** arrange children — for that, compose a `VStack`, `HStack`, or `Grid` inside.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain `<div>` by default — pass `as` for a semantic element when the block represents a landmark (`section`, `aside`, `nav`, `header`, `footer`).
- Background/border tokens are picked so every combination meets WCAG AA on both themes.
- Block adds no roles or ARIA on its own; if it represents a region, set `aria-labelledby` on the element via `as` + a child heading.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use Block to lay out children.** Padding and background, yes — direction, gap, and alignment, no. Wrap a `VStack` / `HStack` / `Grid` inside.
- **Don't add outer margin to the outermost Block.** Spacing between siblings belongs to the parent (a `VStack` `gap`, a `Grid` `gap`).
- **Width defaults to `auto`.** Set `width="full"` if you want it to span the row; set `width="fit"` to collapse to its content.
- **Don't reach for Block when a named Layout exists.** A `Card` is a Block with curated chrome; a `Container` is a Block with width capping. Use the named component when one fits.

components.title: Breadcrumb
components.purpose: `Breadcrumb` shows where the current page sits in the site's hierarchy and links back up it. It helps on deep, structured sites (membership → chapter → sightings → one sighting). It is not a history of where someone has been, and it doesn't replace the main navigation.

guidance.Accessibility:
- A `nav` landmark named "Breadcrumb" (change it with `aria-label`) holding an
  ordered list, so screen readers announce "list, 4 items".
- The current page is the last item, not a link, and has `aria-current="page"`.
- The chevrons between crumbs are decorative and hidden from assistive technology.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't link the current page.** A link to where you already are is a dead end.
- **Don't use a breadcrumb on a flat site.** With one or two levels it is noise.
- **Don't build the trail from browser history.** It shows hierarchy, not the path
  someone took.

components.title: Button
components.purpose: `Button` is the canonical action element — every click that mutates state, confirms a flow, or navigates the user should be a `Button` (or a `Button` with `as="a"` for navigation). For lower-emphasis text actions, drop to `variant="ghost"`; for destructive flows, `variant="danger"`.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a real `<button>` element by default, through React Aria's Button — full keyboard support, correct role, and consistent press handling across mouse, touch and keyboard.
- The focus-visible outline uses `theme.colors.border.focus` with a 2px offset so it stays visible against the button surface.
- `disabled` sets the native `disabled` attribute, taking the button out of the tab order.
- Foreground helpers choose readable text for concrete opaque button surfaces. Their requested contrast is a target, not a guarantee for every custom color; CSS variables and translucent backgrounds require checking the resolved foreground against the rendered surface in each state.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use `ghost` for the primary action.** It reads as a tertiary option; users miss it.
- **Don't stack two `primary` buttons side-by-side.** Pair `primary` with `secondary` or `ghost` so the call-to-action is unambiguous.
- **Don't wrap a `Button` in an `<a>`** — use `as="a"` instead. Nested interactives produce two focus stops and confuse screen readers.
- **`primary` lifts by default, others don't.** Override with `lift={false}` on `primary` if the surrounding density makes the motion feel busy.
guidance.Form and pending-action contract:
`Button` is built on React Aria's Button, so a press works the same with a mouse, touch, keyboard or screen reader, and it defaults to `type="button"`: set `type="submit"` on the single submit action. `onClick` still works (React Aria treats it as `onPress`).

While a request is in flight, set `pending`. The button keeps focus and its place in the tab order, announces that it is busy, and ignores further presses, so the action can't be submitted twice. Keep a stable label or replace it with specific progress text; the consumer still owns recovery after a failed request.

Native `disabled` behavior applies to the default button element. An anchor rendered with `as="a"` does not gain native disabled semantics from that prop; remove the unavailable navigation action or implement its keyboard and pointer policy explicitly. Prefer [Link](?path=/docs/functional-link--docs) for navigation within prose and [ConfirmModal](?path=/docs/functional-modal--docs) when a destructive action needs confirmation.

components.title: Card
components.purpose: `Card` is a themed visual container — background, border, radius, and shadow driven by `variant`. It exposes no layout knobs on purpose: internal padding adapts to the surrounding `Presentation` register, and the arrangement of children is whatever `VStack` / `HStack` / `Grid` / `Block` you put inside. For a card with a hover-lift state, use `InteractiveCard`; for a fully clickable card, use `InteractiveCard as="a"`.
documentationSections: A border and a shadow together

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a real `<section>` by default — counts as a landmark when given an `aria-labelledby` pointing at its heading.
- No interactive behavior — keyboard / focus belong to whatever you put inside (use `InteractiveCard` if the whole card needs to be clickable).
- Card establishes foreground roles against its own background, so default Heading, Text and Link content remains readable in all variants. Code, Kbd and painted controls retain independently calculated foregrounds for their own surfaces. Explicit semantic tones, custom colors and translucent backgrounds still require composition-specific validation.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't reach for a `padding` prop — there isn't one.** Wrap the card (or its ancestor `Section`) in a `Presentation` register; the padding follows.
- **Don't put two cards inside a card.** Nested cards turn into a stack of borders. Use a `VStack` inside one card instead.
- **Don't make a non-interactive `Card` clickable.** A bare `Card` with an `onClick` has no focus, no keyboard support, and no `role="button"`. Use `InteractiveCard` (or wrap in a `Link`).
- **Don't use `featured` for more than one card per group.** Its job is to single out the recommended option — two "recommended" cards mean none of them are.

components.title: Centered
components.purpose: `Centered` centers its children on both axes inside a flex container. Use it whenever you'd otherwise write `display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;` by hand — empty states, loading spinners, "perfectly centered" hero callouts, modal contents. For a centered *column* of items with consistent gaps, use `VStack align="center" justify="center"` instead.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain `<div>` flex container — no roles, no announcements. The centered child supplies its own semantics.
- For a loading state inside Centered, ensure the inner element (e.g. `Spinner`) carries the `role="status"` announcement — Centered is layout only.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't nest Centered inside Centered.** Once you need multiple children with gaps, switch to `VStack align="center" justify="center"`.
- **Pass `minHeight` unless the parent already constrains height.** Without it, Centered collapses to the height of its child and "centering" becomes a no-op.
- **Don't reach for Centered when an empty state is the real intent.** `EmptyState` already centers an icon + title + body + action; use the named component.
- **Centered doesn't add padding.** If the centered child touches the edges, add padding on the parent or wrap in a `Block`.

components.title: Checkbox
components.purpose: `Checkbox` is a controlled boolean input that styles a hidden native `<input type="checkbox">` — you keep full keyboard and screen-reader behavior, plus a tick / dash visual that matches the rest of the library. For an *immediate-effect* toggle (a setting, a preference) use `Switch` instead; for a one-of-many choice use `RadioGroup`.

guidance.Accessibility:
Helper and error text are exposed as descriptions, separate from the visible label. A supplied `aria-describedby` is preserved and combined with the component’s message.

- The visible box is decorative — the real interactive element is the hidden `<input>`, which is fully keyboard-operable (Space toggles, Tab navigates).
- The entire wrapper is a `<label>`, so a label click toggles the input — no `htmlFor` plumbing needed.
- `error` sets `aria-invalid` on the input so assistive tech flags it during form validation.
- The focus ring uses `--squonk-colors-border-focus` and surrounds the visible box, not the hidden input. It shows for keyboard focus only.
- An uncontrolled checkbox returns to `defaultChecked` when its form resets, and a disabled ancestor `<fieldset>` disables it.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use a checkbox for an immediate-effect toggle.** Settings that apply instantly should be a `Switch`. Reserve checkbox for "submit later" or multi-select.
- **Don't render a lone checkbox without a label.** Screen readers can't infer meaning from the box — pass a `label` (or, in tight grids, an `aria-label` via `...inputProps`).
- **Don't forget to forward `onChange`.** The first argument is the new boolean, not the event — read the signature carefully if you're migrating from a raw input.
- **Don't combine `indeterminate` with `checked={true}`.** The component will render the dash, but the semantics are contradictory. Pair `indeterminate` with `checked={false}`.

components.title: CheckboxGroup
components.purpose: `CheckboxGroup` asks one question with several independent answers: "Which accounts do you want to set up?". It keeps the selection as an array of values, names the group with a legend, and puts group-level errors in one place.

guidance.Accessibility:
- A `<fieldset>` named by its legend; helper and error text are its description.
  Each option's own `helperText` describes that checkbox.
- Each option is a native checkbox: Tab moves between them and Space toggles.
- Every checked option submits its `value` under the shared `name`.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use a CheckboxGroup for "pick one".** Checkboxes signal that several
  answers are allowed. Use `RadioGroup`.
- **Don't use a CheckboxGroup for settings that apply immediately.** Use `Switch`es.
- **Don't hide why an option is disabled.** Give it `helperText`.

components.title: Cluster
components.purpose: `Cluster` is a wrapping horizontal flow for a group of small related items — tags, chips, breadcrumbs, button rows, badge sets. Children flow left-to-right and wrap onto the next line as the parent narrows, all with a consistent gap. Reach for `Cluster` when the *intent* is "a loose group that wraps as needed". For a row that should push children to opposite ends without wrapping, use `Split`; for a strict row that never wraps, use `HStack` directly.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain wrapping `<div>` — children supply their own semantics (badge, button, link, breadcrumb).
- Gap is consistent on both axes, so a wrapping cluster doesn't feel cramped on the second line.
- For breadcrumbs, wrap the cluster in a `<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">` to make it a landmark.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use `Cluster` when items should split to opposite ends.** That's `Split` — the intent is different.
- **Don't pack tens of clusters with `gap="xl"`.** Wide gaps look intentional at first and then ridiculous when the cluster wraps. Stick with `xs`–`md` for tag-like content.
- **Don't put block-level children in a Cluster.** It's meant for inline-flow items; full-width cards inside a cluster turn into a sad single column.
- **Don't reproduce a Cluster manually with `HStack` + `wrap`.** That's what `Cluster` is — the named component encodes the recurring intent.

components.title: Code
components.purpose: `Code` renders monospace text — inline by default for command names, file paths, and identifiers; or as a horizontally-scrolling block with `block` for code samples. Pair with `Kbd` when you want to show keyboard input rather than code.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Inline renders as native `<code>`, block as `<pre><code>` — both are announced as code by screen readers.
- Block content preserves whitespace and scrolls horizontally rather than wrapping, so indentation stays readable.
- The contrast between text and the subtle background tint meets WCAG AA on both light and dark themes.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't put long code in inline `Code`.** It won't wrap and will blow out the line height. Switch to `block`.
- **Don't use Code for keyboard shortcuts.** A keystroke is a `Kbd`, not a `Code` — visually distinct, semantically correct.
- **Don't nest Code inside Code.** The styling stacks (double border, double padding). Pick one level.
- **Don't rely on syntax highlighting.** `Code` is unstyled — for highlighted samples, wrap a syntax highlighter inside.

components.title: Container
components.purpose: `Container` caps content width and centers it horizontally. Use it once near the top of a page (inside `Header`, the main content area, and `Footer`) so long-form content doesn't sprawl across a wide monitor. `size` maps to a breakpoint token, so the value of "max" stays consistent if breakpoint primitives are tuned later.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain `<div>` — no roles or ARIA. It's a layout primitive only.
- Use `as` to render a semantic element when the container *is* the landmark (`as="main"`, `as="article"`); otherwise let the surrounding `Page` / `Section` carry the semantics.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't nest Containers.** One sets the max width; nesting a second adds nothing but an indent. If you need an inner narrower column, drop a `Block maxWidth=...` inside.
- **Don't use Container for fixed-width components.** It's a *page-level* layout. A card inside a `VStack` doesn't need its own Container.
- **Don't disable gutters on the outermost Container.** Without horizontal padding, content runs to the edge of the viewport on mobile.
- **Don't pick `wide` by default.** Most reading content benefits from `desktop` or `tablet`; `wide` is for explicit data layouts.

components.title: Currency
components.purpose: `Currency` shows an amount of money, formatted for its currency and locale with the currency's own decimal places: `$1,234.50`, `£1,234.50`, `1.234,50 €`, `￥1,235`. It renders a `<data>` element whose `value` is the plain decimal (`"1234.50"`), so the machine-readable amount travels with the text. It is inline: it takes the surrounding font size, weight and colour, and uses tabular figures so amounts in a column line up. It formats exactly like [CurrencyField](?path=/docs/components-inputs-currency-field--docs), because both use the same helper.
documentationSections: Minor units, bigints and decimal strings

guidance.Accessibility:
- The text is the formatted amount, so screen readers read it with its currency
  (`$12.50`, "twelve dollars fifty"). The `<data>` element adds no role.
- Accounting brackets and compact abbreviations are shown visually, while
  screen readers get the full signed amount (`-$192.82`, `$1,234,567.00`).
- Tones are `Text`'s, which meet contrast on the page and surface in both modes.
  Colour supports the sign; it never replaces it.
- An amount whose meaning depends on its row ("owed", "credit") needs that
  context in the row or column header, not only in colour.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't add money up as floats.** `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`, and
  the error grows over a column. Add integer cents (`toMinorUnits`) and pass the
  total with `minorUnits`, or total on the server.
- **Don't format with `toFixed` or string templates.** `` `$${n.toFixed(2)}` ``
  rounds `1.005` to `1.00`, ignores grouping, and is wrong for JPY and KWD.
- **Don't pass cents without `minorUnits`.** `1999` without it is $1,999.00.
- **Don't drop the sign and rely on colour.** Keep the minus or brackets for
  people who can't tell red from green.
- **Don't leave `locale` to chance in a single-country app.** Without it, an
  en-US browser shows NZD as `NZ$`.
- **Don't use `compact` where the exact amount matters,** such as a payment or a
  return. It rounds to about two significant digits.

components.title: CurrencyField
components.purpose: `CurrencyField` is the input for an amount of money: a payment, a price, a figure on a dues statement. It is built on React Aria's `NumberField`, so it formats and reads amounts with `Intl.NumberFormat`: the symbol, the separators and the decimal places follow the `currency` and the `locale`, and the amount is rounded to the currency's places when it's committed. Type `12.5`, leave the field, and it shows `$12.50`; its value is the number `12.5`.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The label is a real `<label>` for the input, so clicking it focuses the field.
  Give every field a `label`, or an `aria-label` when the label is elsewhere.
- The input is a text box described as a number field. `helperText`, then `error`,
  then the currency code (with `showCurrencyCode`) and any `aria-describedby` you
  pass are read as its description; an error is announced politely when it appears.
- Up and Down arrows step the amount by `step`. The mouse wheel never changes an amount, so scrolling past a focused
  field can't alter a payment.
- On phones the keyboard is the decimal pad, or one with a minus key when
  `allowNegative` is set.
- The value includes the symbol (`$12.50`), so it is read with its currency.
  Don't repeat the currency in the label unless people choose it elsewhere.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use `TextField` with `inputMode="decimal"` for money.** You lose
  formatting, rounding and paste handling, and end up parsing `"$1,234.50"` yourself.
- **Don't add amounts up as floats.** `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. Convert
  with `toMinorUnits(amount, 2)` and add integer cents, or add on the server.
- **Send integer minor units or a decimal string to the server,** not a float:
  `toMinorUnits(12.5, 2)` is `1250`; a form `name` submits `"12.50"`.
- **Don't expect `onChange` on every keystroke.** It fires when the amount is
  committed. Show a running total from committed values, as the dues instalment plan demo does.
- **Don't hard-code `$` in the label or helper text for a multi-currency form.**
  Let the field show the symbol, and use `showCurrencyCode` if dollars could be confused.
- **Don't leave `locale` to chance in a single-country app.** Without it the
  browser decides, and an en-US browser shows NZD as `NZ$`.
- **Don't clamp a rule silently.** `maxValue` quietly lowers an amount; for a
  limit people must know about ("up to what you owe"), validate and show an error.

components.title: Divider
components.purpose: A semantic separator between sibling content. `Divider` renders a native `<hr>` for horizontal lines (the accessible default) and switches to a `<div>` with `role="separator"` and `aria-orientation="vertical"` for vertical ones — `<hr>` has no vertical mode.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The horizontal variant uses `<hr>`, which assistive tech already announces as a separator — no ARIA needed.
- The vertical variant adds `role="separator"` and `aria-orientation="vertical"` so it remains announced after the element change.
- The divider color uses `theme.colors.border.default` — verified to meet WCAG AA contrast against both light and dark backgrounds without being visually loud.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use Divider for decoration.** If the line isn't meaningfully separating content, it's just visual noise — drop it.
- **Vertical dividers need a sized flex parent.** Without one (e.g. `align="stretch"` on an `HStack`), there's no height for the line to take.
- **Don't put a divider above the page footer.** `Footer` already has its own top border; adding a divider creates a double line.
- **Don't pile up dividers between every list item.** That's a `<ul>` with row gaps and (optionally) hover states — not a stack of Dividers.

components.title: DonutChart
components.purpose: `DonutChart` shows how one whole splits into a few parts, as a ring with the total in the middle: dues collected by type, sightings verified against still under review. It works best with two to five parts, where the reader wants the rough share rather than exact comparisons. Angles are hard to compare precisely, so when the parts are close in size, there are more than five, or you need to compare the same split across periods, use a sorted horizontal [BarChart](?path=/docs/functional-bar-chart--docs). For a single value against a target or capacity, use a [Meter](?path=/docs/functional-meter--docs); for a headline number, a [Stat](?path=/docs/functional-stat--docs).

guidance.Accessibility:
- The chart is a `<figure>` named by `title` and described by `description`. `title` is required; `hideTitle` hides it visually only.
- The "Table view" toggle button (`aria-pressed`) swaps the ring for a table of every part, its value and its share, captioned with `title`. It is the dependable way to read exact values with a keyboard, screen reader or magnifier, and it includes any parts folded into "Other".
- The plot is focusable (`role="application"`) and arrow keys move the tooltip between slices.
- Colour never works alone: two or more parts get a legend, the tooltip names each part, and the table labels every row. Light-mode slots 3 to 5 are under 3:1 contrast on white, which is why the legend and table view are always present.
- The total and its label are text, never coloured to match a slice.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Too many parts.** Past five, slices get thin and similar colours sit side by side. Use a sorted horizontal BarChart.
- **Comparing two donuts.** Reading the change in a slice's angle between two rings is guesswork. Show the same split across periods as a stacked BarChart.
- **Parts that don't make a whole.** A donut says "these add up to the total". Overlapping categories (a member can hold both a Keeper and a Life membership) belong in a BarChart.
- **Unsorted parts.** Without an order, the ring is hard to scan and the wrong parts fold into "Other". Sort largest first.
- **Hiding the folded parts.** If "Other" holds something people need, a donut is the wrong chart.
- **Colouring the legend or total text.** Text stays in text colours; the swatch carries the colour.
- **A donut for a single value against a target.** "72% of sightings verified" is a Meter, not a two-slice ring.

components.title: Drawer
components.purpose: `Drawer` slides a panel in from the edge of the screen for a task or detail that needs more room than a `Popover`, while keeping the page beside it in view: editing a record from a list, a case's details, filters on a phone. It behaves like a `Modal`: focus stays inside until it closes.

guidance.Accessibility:
- A modal `dialog` named by `title`. Focus moves into it on open, stays inside
  while open, and returns to the control that opened it on close.
- Escape and a backdrop press request close through `onClose`; the page behind is
  hidden from assistive technology and doesn't scroll.
- The slide animation is removed when people ask for reduced motion.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use a Drawer for primary navigation on desktop.** Keep navigation visible.
- **Don't stack Drawers.** Open a Modal from a Drawer for a confirmation, not
  another Drawer.
- **Don't lose work on close.** Confirm before discarding changes.

components.title: DropdownMenu
components.purpose: `DropdownMenu` is a trigger button with an attached menu of actions — the primitive behind user menus, row-action menus, and "…" overflow menus. It owns the open/close behaviour (click, outside-press, `Escape`) unless you control it via `open` / `onOpenChange`, and implements the WAI-ARIA menu-button keyboard pattern.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The trigger is a real `<button>` with `aria-haspopup="menu"` /
  `aria-expanded`; the panel is `role="menu"` with `role="menuitem"` children.
- `Enter` / `Space` / `ArrowDown` open the menu and focus the first item;
  `ArrowUp` opens and focuses the last. Arrows move focus between items,
  typing jumps to a matching item, `Home` / `End` jump, `Enter` activates,
  `Escape` and `Tab` close, and closing refocuses the trigger.
- Focus moves onto each item (roving focus), so screen readers announce items
  as you move. Disabled items are skipped. Opened by pointer, the menu itself
  takes focus and items follow the pointer; the first arrow key focuses the
  first item.
- The panel fades and scales in and out; reduced-motion users get no
  animation.
guidance.Pitfalls:
- Don't nest another `<button>` inside `trigger` — the trigger already renders
  one. Use `<Button as="span">` if you want button styling inside it.
- The panel opens below the trigger and flips or shifts to stay inside the
  viewport. It renders in a portal on `<body>`, so an ancestor with
  `overflow: hidden` never clips it.
guidance.Placement contract: The menu renders in a portal on `<body>` and is positioned against its trigger, with `align` choosing the start or end edge (following writing direction). It flips and shifts around viewport collisions, and overflow ancestors can't clip it.

components.title: EmptyState
components.purpose: `EmptyState` is the centered "no data yet" composition: an optional illustration, a title, optional sub-copy, and an optional call-to-action. Use it anywhere a list, table, dashboard panel, or search result has no content to show — the user sees *why* the surface is empty and *what to do about it*, not a blank rectangle.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The `icon` slot is wrapped in `aria-hidden="true"` — the meaning lives in the title and body, not the picture.
- Internally renders a `Heading level={3}` for the title; if the empty state is the page's primary content, wrap it in a `Presentation` register and use `as="h1"` on a parent heading if needed.
- Body copy uses `tone="secondary"` for the typical "supporting" weight, which still meets WCAG AA.
- The action slot is whatever you pass — make sure it's a real button or link, not a clickable `<div>`.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't ship an empty state without a next step.** "No projects" is a complaint; "No projects — start one →" is a UI. Pair every empty state with either an action or a clear "this is fine" message.
- **Don't pile up multiple primary buttons.** One primary action; everything else is `secondary` or `ghost`. The whole point is to point the user at *the* next step.
- **Don't use a giant illustration in a small panel.** EmptyState centers; in a tight container the illustration crowds the copy. Shrink the icon or drop it.
- **Don't reuse first-run copy for filter-results.** "No projects yet — create one" makes no sense after the user filtered to "archived = true". Distinguish the two states.

components.title: Fieldset
components.purpose: `Fieldset` groups related fields under a legend: an address, contact details, a section of a long form. Screen readers announce the legend when focus enters the group, so "Postcode" is heard as "Postal address, Postcode".

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a native `<fieldset>` named by its `<legend>`. Helper and error text are
  its description.
- `hideLegend` hides the legend visually but keeps it for screen readers. Use it
  only when a visible heading right above already says the same thing.
- Don't nest fieldsets more than one level deep; the repeated legends become noise.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use a Fieldset just for spacing.** It adds a named group to the
  accessibility tree. Use `VStack` to space unrelated fields.
- **Don't put the only instructions in the legend.** Keep it to a name and put
  guidance in `helperText`.

components.title: Footer
components.purpose: `Footer` renders the bottom landmark of a page — semantic `<footer>`, surface background, top border, smaller text scale. Like `Header`, it's a content-agnostic shell; the consumer composes what goes inside (copyright, links, address, social). Layout knobs are deliberately absent: use a `Split` / `Cluster` / `Grid` inside to control "copyright left, links right" or "three-column nav".

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a native `<footer>` landmark — at the top level of the page, screen readers announce it as `contentinfo`.
- A `<footer>` nested inside an `<article>` or `<section>` is a *section* footer, not the page contentinfo — still valid HTML, just not a landmark.
- Text contrast uses `theme.colors.text.secondary` against the surface background — verified to meet WCAG AA on both themes.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't pin the Footer to the bottom of the viewport.** A footer that always shows is a *toolbar*, not a footer. Let it sit at the natural end of the page.
- **Don't ship multiple page-level Footers.** One per page; multiple `<footer>` elements without a containing landmark confuse screen-reader navigation.
- **Don't hardcode width inside.** Wrap link groups in a `Container` so wide monitors don't stretch the footer's link list into a thin ribbon.
- **Don't use `tone="page"` on the default theme.** It only helps when your page background is itself a strong color. On the standard white/dark page the surface tint *is* the visual separator.

components.title: Form
components.purpose: `@squonk/ui/form` builds forms on [TanStack Form](https://tanstack.com/form) with the library's fields already wired up: values, blur state and errors. Validate with any [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) library; the examples use [Zod](https://zod.dev). Every form gets the same behaviour:

guidance.Accessibility:
- `form.Form` sets `noValidate`, so the browser's own error bubbles don't compete.
- The error summary takes focus after a failed submit, so screen-reader users hear
  "There is a problem" and the list. Each link moves focus to its field.
- Each field's error is its description and sets `aria-invalid`.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't validate on the first keystroke.** The bound fields wait for blur;
  don't show your own errors earlier.
- **Don't disable the submit button until the form is valid.** People can't find
  out what's wrong.
- **Don't leave out the error summary on long forms.** It is the only place a
  screen-reader user hears every problem at once.

components.title: Grid
components.purpose: `Grid` is a thin wrapper around CSS Grid with theme-driven gap tokens, responsive column maps, and an auto-fit mode. Use it when content is two-dimensional — cards in a gallery, fields in a form, items in a dashboard. For a single row or column, prefer `VStack` / `HStack`.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain `<div>` — semantics come from what you put inside.
- For a list of equivalent items, wrap each Grid child in an `<li>` and pass `as="ul"` to the Grid so screen-reader users get the list count.
- Grid is purely visual layout; the source DOM order is the reading order, so make sure the source order is sensible.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't fight the grid with margins.** Spacing is `gap` only.
- **Don't reach for a `rows` prop yet.** The library tracks the 95% case (columns, equal rows). If you need explicit row sizing, drop down to `style={{ gridTemplateRows: ... }}`.
- **`minColumnWidth` wins over `columns`** when both are set.
- **Don't use Grid for a single row.** That's an `HStack`. Grid implies "two dimensional"; using it for a one-line row is overkill and obscures intent.

components.title: Header
components.purpose: `Header` renders the top landmark of a page — semantic `<header>`, full width, bottom border, container padding, and a built-in `Presentation` register (defaults to `compact`, since headers are usually utility-dense). Like `Footer`, it's content-agnostic: slot in your logo, nav, search, user menu, and arrange them with a `Split` / `Cluster` inside. Companions: `FixedHeader` pins to the viewport, `StickyHeader` sticks when its parent scrolls.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a native `<header>` landmark — screen readers announce it as the page banner when it's the top-level header.
- Only one top-level `<header>` per page becomes the banner landmark; nested `<header>` elements inside `<article>` or `<section>` are valid but not landmarks.
- `FixedHeader` uses `theme.zIndices.fixed`; `StickyHeader` uses `theme.zIndices.sticky` — both sit below modals and popovers.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't hardcode the header height.** It sizes itself from content + register padding — let it flex when you add a search box or a tall logo.
- **Don't ship multiple page-level Headers.** Pick one (Header, FixedHeader, or StickyHeader) per page.
- **Don't forget the spacer under a `FixedHeader`.** Without it, page content sits behind the header on initial load.
- **Don't wrap header content in another `Presentation`.** `Header` already sets the register — re-wrapping fights the inheritance.

components.title: Heading
components.purpose: `Heading` renders semantic `h1`–`h6` elements with consistent visual sizing. By default `level` drives both the rendered tag *and* the visual scale; use `as` to detach them when the document outline needs a different tag than the visual rank (e.g. an SEO `h1` that looks like an `h4`). The actual font size for a given level depends on the surrounding `Presentation` register.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The rendered tag is always `h1`–`h6` (or whatever you pass to `as`) — never a `<div>` masquerading as a heading.
- Heading levels are landmarks for screen-reader navigation. Don't skip levels (`h1` then `h3`) — it confuses outline traversal.
- Every page should have exactly one `h1`; the page's title or hero usually owns it.
- The `<em>` accent is purely visual; screen readers still announce it as emphasized text, which is normally what you want.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't pick a heading level for its size.** Use `level` for semantics; use `as` + `level` if you need to detach visual from outline. Skipping levels for visual reasons breaks screen-reader navigation.
- **Don't ship more than one `h1` per page.** Use `as="h2"` (or a smaller level) for repeated section headings.
- **Don't override `<em>` color.** It's tied to `theme.colors.primary` for the brand accent pattern — restyling it locally fights the system.
- **Don't put body copy inside a Heading.** Headings are short, scannable labels. Run-on headings hurt outline navigation.

components.title: HStack
components.purpose: `HStack` arranges its children horizontally (left to right) with a token-driven gap and sensible alignment props. It is **not** a styled container — no padding, border, or background, only arrangement. For vertical arrangement use `VStack`; for wrapping rows of chips/tags use `Cluster`; for "leading group | trailing group" use `Split`.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain `<div>` — no roles, no announcements. Children supply their own semantics.
- DOM order is reading order; the visual `justify="between"` doesn't change traversal.
- For a row of equivalent navigation items, render as `<nav>` (`as="nav"`) and use a child `<ul>` for the list count.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't add margins to children.** The whole point of HStack is that the parent owns the spacing. If you find yourself reaching for `margin-right` on a child, change the `gap` instead.
- **`align="center"` is the default.** Children align to the row centerline. Switch to `align="start"` to top-align them.
- **Need vertical arrangement?** Use `VStack` — they are peer components, not variants of one another.
- **Don't reach for HStack when a named composition exists.** A `Cluster` is HStack-with-wrap; a `Split` is HStack-with-justify-between; a `MediaObject` is HStack-with-content-stack. Use the named one when it fits.

components.title: Icon
components.purpose: The library's curated icon set. Each icon is a named component — `SearchIcon`, `CloseIcon`, `WarningIcon` — named for what it means, not what it looks like, so the drawing behind a name can change without breaking your code. Import only the icons you use; the rest stay out of your bundle.

guidance.Accessibility:
- An icon next to text is decorative: leave out `label` and it is hidden from
  assistive technology (`aria-hidden`).
- An icon that carries meaning on its own — a status mark with no text — needs a
  `label`, which makes it `role="img"` with that name.
- An icon-only button needs a name on the **button** (`aria-label`), not the icon.
- Icons use `currentColor`, so they follow the text colour and dark mode.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't import from `react-icons` in your app to add one-off icons.** Ask for
  the icon in the library so it is reviewed and named once.
- **Don't use an icon as the only label of a control** unless the control has an
  `aria-label`, and prefer visible text for anything people must learn.
- **Don't resize with CSS `font-size` tricks inside controls;** use
  `size="control"`.

components.title: IconButton
components.purpose: `IconButton` is a square button that shows only an icon: toolbar actions, row actions in a table, a close button, a "more" menu trigger. Its `label` is the button's accessible name and, by default, appears in a tooltip, so nobody has to guess what the icon means.

guidance.Accessibility:
- `label` is required and becomes `aria-label`. Describe the action and its object
  ("Delete draft", not "Trash"), especially when a row repeats the same icon.
- The icon is decorative (`aria-hidden`).
- The tooltip opens on hover and keyboard focus and is announced as a description.
  Set `tooltip={false}` when the label is already visible nearby, or when you wrap
  the button in your own `Tooltip` with longer text.
- Defaults to `type="button"`, so it never submits a form by accident.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't disable an IconButton to explain something.** A disabled button gets no
  hover or focus, so its tooltip never shows. Hide the action or explain nearby.
- **Don't use an obscure icon to save space.** If people need the tooltip to know
  what it does, use a text `Button` instead.
- **Don't wrap an IconButton in another Tooltip without `tooltip={false}`,** or two
  hints compete.

components.title: Illustration
components.purpose: Small spot illustrations for the moments a screen needs a picture: an empty list, a search with no results, a step finished, a feature on a landing page. They're drawn in one style (ink outlines, paper and tint fills, one accent touch), and every colour comes from the theme, so they follow your brand and the colour mode with no extra work.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Most illustrations repeat what the heading or message beside them says. Leave
  `label` out and the illustration is hidden from assistive technology.
- When the picture carries meaning nothing else says, give it a `label`: it
  becomes an image with that name.
- Never put the only instruction or status in an illustration; say it in text.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Using an illustration as an icon.** Icons sit inside controls and lines of
  text; illustrations sit beside content. Use `Icon` components in buttons,
  fields and menus.
- **Recolouring with CSS.** Re-point the `components.illustration.*` tokens (or
  the roles they follow) instead, so every illustration changes together.
- **Importing `ILLUSTRATIONS` for one picture.** It brings in every drawing;
  import the named component.

components.title: InfiniteList
components.purpose: `InfiniteList` loads more as people scroll, with no button to press. It suits feeds people browse from newest to oldest (membership activity, notifications, a case's history). For records people search for and come back to ("it was on page 3"), use `Pagination` or a `Table` with `pageSize`.
documentationSections: The end, and nothing at all

guidance.Accessibility:
Infinite scrolling is hard for keyboard and screen-reader users, so this follows
the WAI-ARIA **feed** pattern:

- The list is a `feed` named by `aria-label`, and `aria-busy` while loading. Each
  item is an `<article>` with `aria-posinset` and `aria-setsize` ("4 of 120";
  pass `total` when you know it).
- **Page Down** and **Page Up** move focus between articles.
- **Ctrl+End** and **Ctrl+Home** jump out of the feed, so the page footer and
  everything after the list stay reachable however much has loaded.
- A polite status line announces "Loading more…" and then "Loaded 12 more".
- Give each item a heading so screen-reader users can skim with heading navigation.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use it for search results or tables people act on.** They lose their place
  when they come back, and can't tell anyone where a record was.
- **Don't put essential links in the page footer below an infinite list.** People
  using a mouse may never reach it; keep them in the header or navigation.
- **Don't load on every scroll event.** Leave the timing to the list; just append
  the page in `onLoadMore`.

components.title: Inline
components.purpose: `Inline` is an `inline-flex` group — it sits **in text flow** without breaking the line. Use it for label-with-icon, chip-with-badge, text-with-trailing-action, keyboard combinations, and anywhere a small horizontal group needs to participate in its surrounding prose. `align` defaults to `baseline` so the group aligns with the text baseline of the container. For block-level horizontal groups (own row, not flowing with text), use `HStack`.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders an inline `<span>` so it doesn't disrupt the surrounding paragraph or list semantics.
- Children supply their own semantics — `Kbd`, `<a>`, icons with `aria-hidden`.
- `align="baseline"` is the default because Inline is typically used inside prose; the baseline alignment keeps the group visually anchored to the text.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use Inline for layouts that take their own row.** Use `HStack` — it's `display: flex` and gives the row its own block-flow context. - **`align="baseline"` is the default.** Override to `align="center"` only when there's no surrounding text to align against. - **Don't put block-level children inside Inline.** A `

` or `

` inside an inline-flex span breaks the inline flow. Stick to spans, anchors, icons, and `Kbd`. - **Don't nest Inlines deeply.** One level for a small group is the intent; nested Inlines turn into a debugging puzzle.

components.title: InteractiveCard
components.purpose: `InteractiveCard` is `Card` plus a hover-lift state — it slightly rises and casts a shadow on hover, signalling "this responds to interaction." Use it for a card that links somewhere (`as="a" href="…"`) or opens a detail panel on click. For a static, non-interactive card use `Card` instead — reserving the lift for things that actually do something keeps the cue meaningful.

guidance.Accessibility:
- When `as="a"`, the card behaves like any link: focusable via Tab, activatable via Enter, and announced by screen readers using its accessible name (the visible text content).
- The `&:focus-visible` state renders `theme.colors.border.focus` as a 2px outline — don't suppress it with a custom `outline: none`.
- Use `as="button" onClick={...}` for an action. Native buttons already provide Tab, Enter and Space behavior; do not add redundant keyboard handlers. The default type is `button`; opt into `type="submit"` explicitly for a form submission.
- A native element such as the default section with `onClick` gains `role="button"`, `tabIndex={0}`, Enter activation and Space activation on release. Caller keyboard handlers can prevent the default activation. Custom routing components retain their own semantics.
- Supply clear visible action text or an `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby`. Bubbled clicks from nested controls do not activate the card; keyboard activation applies only when the card itself has focus. Prefer separate sibling actions because a button role can flatten descendant semantics for assistive technology.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't nest another interactive element inside an anchor or button card.** Nested buttons/links create invalid or ambiguous native interaction. If the card needs a secondary action, put it visually inside but move it outside the anchor in the DOM, or reconsider the composition.
- **Don't use `InteractiveCard` for a card that doesn't do anything on click.** If there's no navigation or handler, the hover-lift is a promise the UI doesn't keep — use `Card`.
- **Don't override `text-decoration`.** It's already suppressed for the `as="a"` case; re-adding an underline via a wrapper style fights the component's intent.

components.title: Kbd
components.purpose: `Kbd` displays a keystroke or chord — a single key or a combo. Use it in documentation, tooltips, empty-state hints, and command-palette UIs. For code (commands, file paths, identifiers) use `Code` instead — the visual treatments are deliberately different so the reader can tell a key from a token.
documentationSections: Shortcut behavior belongs to the application

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders native `<kbd>` markup to identify keyboard input; actual announcement varies by browser and assistive technology.
- The "raised" appearance comes from a slightly heavier bottom border and inset shadow. Check key-label contrast after changing theme tokens.
- Use platform-appropriate key names. Explain unfamiliar symbols such as `⌘` as Command in surrounding text or an accessible description.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't put `+` between Kbds.** The space between two `<Kbd>` elements already reads as a chord. `<Kbd>⌘</Kbd> + <Kbd>K</Kbd>` adds noise.
- **Don't use Kbd for code or commands.** Use `Code` for `npm install`; use `Kbd` for the keys you press.
- **Don't wrap multi-key chords in a single Kbd.** `<Kbd>⌘K</Kbd>` reads as one key. Split them: `<Kbd>⌘</Kbd> <Kbd>K</Kbd>`.
- **Don't use Kbd for non-keyboard hints.** Mouse buttons and gestures aren't keys — use plain prose or a custom icon.

components.title: LineChart
components.purpose: `LineChart` shows how one to eight measures change over an ordered axis, usually time: dues collected by month, sightings logged by week. Each series is one line; hover, or focus the plot and use the arrow keys, to read every value at a point, and the "Table view" toggle swaps the plot for a table of all of them. It is not for unordered categories (chapters, account types): a line between Auckland and Otago implies a trend that isn't there, so use a [BarChart](?path=/docs/functional-bar-chart--docs). For volumes where the area under the line means "how much", use an [AreaChart](?path=/docs/functional-area-chart--docs); for a trend beside a single figure, a [Sparkline](?path=/docs/functional-sparkline--docs).

guidance.Accessibility:
- The chart is a `<figure>` named by `title` and described by `description`. `title` is required even with `hideTitle`, which hides it visually only.
- The "Table view" toggle is a toggle button (`aria-pressed`) that swaps the plot for a table of every value, captioned with `title`. It is the dependable way to read exact values with a keyboard, a screen reader or a magnifier.
- The plot is focusable (`role="application"`). Arrow keys step through the points and show the tooltip for each, so nothing is reachable only by hovering.
- Colour never works alone. Two or more series get a legend, the tooltip names each series, and the table labels every column. Light-mode slots 3 to 5 are under 3:1 contrast on white, which is why the legend and table view are always there.
- Text is never drawn in a series colour: titles, ticks, legend labels and tooltip values stay in text colours. Don't colour a heading or caption to match a line.
- Write `formatValue` so values are read with their unit ("$58,300"), not as bare numbers.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Two value axes.** The chart has one value axis and no dual-axis option. Plotting dollars against a count on one chart invites false correlations; use two charts side by side.
- **A line across unordered categories.** Chapters or dues types have no order to trend across. Use a BarChart.
- **More than eight series.** Only the first eight are drawn. Fold the long tail into "Other", or use small multiples.
- **A rainbow of series.** Every series competes for attention. Highlight the one or two that matter and fold the rest, or move them to their own chart.
- **Colours shifting under a filter.** Without `slot`, removing the first series hands its colour to the next. Pin slots when series can be toggled.
- **Colouring text to match a series.** Series colours are for marks; text in slots 3 to 5 fails contrast. Name the series in words.
- **Filling gaps with zero.** A missing month is `null`, not `0`.
- **Smoothing sparse data.** `monotone` on six points suggests readings between them that don't exist. Use `linear` with `showPoints`.

components.title: Link
components.purpose: `Link` is a themed anchor with consistent color, focus ring, and underline policy across the library. Use it for *navigation* — anything that changes the URL. For actions that mutate state, use `Button` (or `Button as="a"` when a CTA looks like a link but acts like a button). For off-site destinations set `external` so the browser opens a new tab and ships safe `rel` attributes.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a real `<a>` by default — full browser affordances (middle-click, copy URL, right-click menu).
- `:focus-visible` outline uses `theme.colors.border.focus` so keyboard users always see the active link.
- Color is paired with the underline policy — color alone never carries the "this is a link" signal in body copy (use `underline="always"`).
- `external` sets `rel="noopener noreferrer"` to prevent `window.opener` exploitation and keep referrer policy tight.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use Link for actions.** Clicking should change the URL. If it submits a form or mutates state, use `Button`.
- **Don't drop the underline in body copy.** `underline="never"` on inline prose hides the link from anyone who isn't hovering — fine for nav, harmful in an article.
- **Don't set `target="_blank"` without `external`.** It works, but you lose the safe `rel` attributes. Use `external` so both happen together.
- **Don't nest a Link inside a Button (or vice versa).** Two interactive elements at the same spot break focus order and screen-reader announcements. Pick one.

components.title: MediaObject
components.purpose: `MediaObject` is the canonical "image-on-the-left, content-on-the-right" shape — list items, comment rows, profile cards, file rows. The media slot stays fixed-size; the content area takes whatever width remains and wraps cleanly. Reach for `MediaObject` whenever you'd otherwise write `<HStack>` with one fixed-width item and a `VStack` beside it — the named component encodes the recurring pattern.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain row — semantics come from what you put in the slots. For a list of MediaObjects, wrap in a `<ul>` and each row in an `<li>` so screen-reader users can navigate the list.
- The media slot doesn't get any special role; an `<Avatar>` inside already carries `role="img"` + `aria-label`.
- For interactive rows (clickable comments, file links), wrap the whole MediaObject in a `Link` or `InteractiveCard` so the entire row is one focus stop, not two.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't put a wide media item in the media slot.** It's meant for fixed-size icons/avatars (typically 24–64px). A 200px-wide thumbnail breaks the pattern — use a `Split` or `Grid` instead.
- **Don't use `align="center"` for multi-line content.** Centering pushes the avatar to the vertical middle, which looks lopsided when the content is 3+ lines. Use `align="start"`.
- **Don't ship MediaObject rows without any vertical separator in a long list.** A `VStack gap="md"` is the minimum; a `Divider` between rows is often better for scannability.
- **Don't reproduce MediaObject manually with HStack + VStack.** That's literally what it is — the named component makes the pattern obvious.

components.title: Meter
components.purpose: `Meter` shows an amount within a known range: storage used, a credit limit drawn, instalments paid, a quota spent. It is built on React Aria's Meter. It is not for work in progress: when something is moving toward completion (an upload, an import), use [ProgressBar](?path=/docs/functional-progress-bar--docs). A meter can sit still at 70% forever; a progress bar that stops moving looks broken. For several amounts to compare against each other, use a [BarChart](?path=/docs/functional-bar-chart--docs).

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders `role="meter"` with `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax`, `aria-valuenow` and `aria-valuetext` (your `valueLabel`, or the percentage).
- Give it a name: a visible `label` (wired up as its label) or `ariaLabel`. A nameless meter is announced as just a number.
- The warning and critical colours are not announced. Put the level in `valueLabel` ("nearing limit") or in nearby text, so it reaches screen reader users and people who can't tell the colours apart.
- It isn't interactive or focusable; screen readers reach it while reading the page.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Using Meter for progress.** If the amount is heading toward "done", use ProgressBar; `role="meter"` tells assistive technology the value is a measurement, not a task status.
- **Colour as the only warning.** A red fill without words leaves some people guessing. Say "at limit" or what to do next.
- **Thresholds as percentages when the range isn't 0–100.** With `maxValue={10000}`, `criticalAt={95}` triggers at $95. Give thresholds in the same units as `value`.
- **A bare percentage for a quantity people know in units.** "70%" of a storage quota is less useful than "42 of 60 GB". Set `valueLabel`.
- **Values outside the range.** An amount over the limit pins the fill at 100%; say how far over in `valueLabel` ("$10,400 of $10,000, $400 over").

components.title: Modal
components.purpose: `Modal` is a centered dialog over a dimmed backdrop, rendered in a portal on `document.body`. It is fully controlled: the consumer owns `open` and gets asked to close via `onClose` — fired by the backdrop press, `Escape`, or the × button.

guidance.Accessibility:
- `role="dialog"`. Instead of `aria-modal` (which trips a Safari focus bug),
  the rest of the page is hidden from assistive technology while it is open.
- Supply a meaningful `title`, `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby`; an explicit
  accessible name takes precedence over the visual title. Untitled dialogs
  fall back to the generic name "Dialog", which consumers should replace with
  the task name.
- Focus moves to the dialog on open, `Tab` cycles within it (skipping
  controls in a disabled fieldset), and focus returns to the previously focused element on close.
- While a dialog is open, the page behind it is hidden from assistive
  technology and its scrolling is locked.
- The dialog and backdrop fade in and out; reduced-motion users get no
  animation.
- `Escape` requests close only on the top dialog. An inner menu consumes Escape
  first. Focus stays in the top dialog and page scroll remains locked until the
  last dialog closes, including when a lower dialog closes first.
guidance.Pitfalls:
- The consumer owns `open` — `onClose` is a *request*, not a state change. If
  you ignore it, the modal stays up (that's how "must choose" dialogs work:
  pass `closeOnBackdrop={false}` and `showCloseButton={false}` too).
- Prefer sequencing dialogs. When a secondary dialog is necessary, closing it
  returns focus to its opener in the remaining dialog; closing the last dialog
  restores the original page focus when that element still exists.

components.title: Motion
components.purpose: Every animation and transition in the library comes from these components. Components don't declare motion in their own styles: they wrap the element that moves. So menus, dialogs and drawers all move alike, every timing comes from the [motion purposes](?path=/docs/foundations-motion--docs), and reduced motion is handled in one place.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Motion never carries meaning on its own: the end state is always readable,
  and content stays usable if an animation never runs.
- Every timing comes from a motion purpose, so a theme can slow everything down,
  and the motion level can reduce it or switch it off.
- `Count` speaks only its final value; `Presence` ignores pointer events while
  it leaves.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Writing a transition in a component's stylesheet.** `npm run lint` fails on
  `transition`, `animation` and `@keyframes` in component CSS; wrap the element
  in a Motion component instead.
- **Wrapping a fragment or text.** Each Motion component needs exactly one
  element child that accepts a `className` (`Presence`, `Swap`, `Reveal` and
  `Layout` also need it to accept `style` or `ref`).
- **Unmounting what Presence should remove.** `{open && <Motion.Presence …>}`
  can't play an exit; keep it mounted and turn `show` off.
- **Animating content people are working with.** Fields, table rows and text
  someone is reading shouldn't move; animate arrivals, not work.

components.title: NavList
components.purpose: Navigation between the pages of an app, marking the one you're on. Use it in a `Sidebar` for an app's main navigation, or across the top of a section for its sub-pages.
documentationSections: How the current page is marked

guidance.Accessibility:
- `label` names the navigation; a page often has several, so it's required.
- The current page has `aria-current="page"`, so screen readers announce it.
- Links are in the tab order, and Enter follows them. Focus shows the theme's
  focus ring, separate from the current-page mark.
- The current page is marked by more than colour: its label is stronger, and
  the bar, underline or ring is a shape.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Styling the current page in app CSS.** Set `indicatorStyle` or re-point
  `roles.indicator.*` so every navigation agrees.
- **Using it for tabs.** Tabs switch content in place and have their own
  keyboard pattern; use `Tabs`.
- **Leaving `current` unset.** Without it, no page is marked as the one
  you're on.

components.title: NetworkGraph
components.purpose: `NetworkGraph` draws things as nodes and the relationships between them as arrows, and arranges them so that connected things sit together. The reader can pan, zoom and select a node to see what it connects to. `NetworkGraphLegend` is its key, and can hide and show each kind of node and link.
documentationSections: When to use a graph, and when a table or list is better

guidance.Accessibility:
- **Name the graph.** `label` is required and names both the graph and its tables. Say what the nodes and links are: "Funding and map sharing between chapters in the Waikato region", not "Graph".
- **Every node is a button** named with its label, its kind, its `description` and how many connections it has ("Waikato Chapter, Chapter, 5 connections"). `aria-pressed` says whether it is selected.
- **Keyboard.** The graph is one tab stop. Inside it:

  | Key | Does |
  | --- | --- |
  | Arrow keys | Move to the connected node that lies most nearly in that direction. Nothing happens when no linked node lies that way. |
  | Page Down, Page Up | Move to the next or previous node in the order of `nodes`, so nodes with no links can be reached |
  | Home, End | Move to the first or last node |
  | Enter, Space | Select the focused node, or clear it if it is already selected |
  | Escape | Clear the selection |
  | P | Pin or unpin the focused node, when pinning is on |

  A focused node shows its links' labels and lights the `hoverHighlight` structure, and the view pans to keep it in sight. A pinned node's name ends in "pinned". Zoom in, Zoom out and Fit to view are buttons after the drawing.
- **The same data as tables.** Screen readers get two visually hidden tables after the drawing: the nodes (name, kind, description, what each connects to) and the links (from, to, relationship). They list what is on show, so a hidden kind is left out of them too.
- **Not colour alone.** Kinds differ by shape, dashed nodes and links by their line, the selection by a ring and bold text, a hidden legend entry by a strike-through. Give each kind its own `shape`, and explain a dashed node in its `description`.
- **Motion.** With the `static` layout, the layout is worked out before anything is drawn, so nothing moves while the reader looks at it. With `force`, nodes move only while the reader drags one. New nodes fade in; with reduced motion, or motion turned off, they are simply there. Link animations stop under reduced motion.
- **Pointer.** Drag pans (or moves a node, when nodes are draggable), the wheel and a pinch zoom. Moving a node is never the only way to reach information: every node stays reachable from the keyboard. While the pointer is over the graph the wheel zooms it instead of scrolling the page, so do not make the graph taller than the screen.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Using a graph as a lookup.** If people come to find one chapter and read its details, give them a searchable Table, and at most a small graph of that chapter's neighbourhood.
- **Too many nodes.** Hundreds of nodes make a hairball that shows nothing. Filter before you draw: one neighbourhood, one kind, one time period.
- **Colour as the only difference between kinds.** Set a `shape` for each kind. About one in twelve men cannot tell some of the palette's colours apart.
- **A status tone for a category.** `tone="error"` on a kind called "Chapter" tells the reader something is wrong. Keep tones for statuses and let categories take the palette.
- **Unstable ids.** If a node's `id` changes between updates (an array index, a new random id), the graph treats it as a new node and it moves. Use the record's own key.
- **No height.** The graph fills its container. In a container with no height it falls back to 160px, which is too small for more than a handful of nodes.
- **A row of flex items with no width.** The graph takes the width it is given and has no width of its own, so in a row (`HStack`) give it or its wrapper a width.
- **Meaning in position.** The layout only keeps linked things close. Left, right, up and down mean nothing, and a node near the middle is not more important. If order or rank matters, use a Table or a list.
- **Motion everywhere.** Animate the links that carry something now, not every link. A graph where everything moves draws the eye nowhere.
- **Meaning only in motion, weight or size.** Reduced motion stops the animation, and widths and sizes are hard to compare. Put the number or the state in the label or `description` too.
- **Every link labelled.** Label the links that carry a detail. A link with no `label` shows its kind's name, which is usually enough.

components.title: Page
components.purpose: `Page` is the outermost container for an application screen — a `<main>` landmark sized to the full viewport (`100vw` × `100vh`), painted with the theme's default background, and set up as a flex row so a `Sidebar` and the main content area drop in side-by-side. It owns vertical scroll for the whole screen; nested scroll areas should be `ScrollBox`, not raw overflow.
documentationSections: A background image from the theme

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a `<main>` landmark by default — screen-reader users can jump straight to the main content via the "main" landmark.
- The full-viewport sizing means the page itself owns vertical scrolling — nested scroll regions should be explicit (`ScrollBox`) so screen readers can identify them.
- Pair `Page` with a `Header` at the top and a `Footer` at the bottom for the standard landmark trio (banner / main / contentinfo).
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't ship multiple `Page` elements per screen.** It's the outermost container; nesting two creates duplicate `<main>` landmarks and double-scroll bugs.
- **Don't add `overflow: hidden` to children.** Vertical scroll lives on `Page` itself; clipping a child breaks scroll-to-anchor and breaks sticky positioning.
- **Don't use the default viewport sizing for a constrained documentation embed.** Override width and height against a definite-size parent as described below.
- **Don't pair `Page` with `position: fixed` content without setting a z-index.** Fixed elements sit on top of the page's scroll container; use the `zIndices.fixed` token to stay consistent with `FixedHeader`.

components.title: Pagination
components.purpose: `Pagination` moves through a long list a page at a time. Use it when people need to know where they are in a large set, come back to the same place, or jump to the end: search results, a history of notices, an audit log. For short lists, show everything; for feeds people only scroll through, a "Show more" button is simpler.

guidance.Accessibility:
- A `nav` landmark named "Pagination". Give it a more specific `aria-label`
  ("Notices pages") when a page has more than one.
- Page buttons are named "Page 3"; the last is "Page 12, last page". The current
  page has `aria-current="page"`.
- Previous and Next are disabled at the ends (`aria-disabled` links in link mode).
- After a page change, the list changes but focus stays on the pagination. If the
  list is long, move focus to its heading or first item so people don't have to
  scroll back up.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't page a short list.** Under about 50 rows, show them all.
- **Don't reset the page silently.** When filters change the total, go back to
  page 1 and say so with the range text.
- **Don't use button pages for results people share.** Use `getPageUrl`.

components.title: Popover
components.purpose: `Popover` shows a small panel next to the control that opened it: an explanation with a link, a few filters, a person's contact details. Unlike a `Tooltip`, it opens on a click and can hold links, buttons and form fields. Unlike a `Modal`, the page behind stays usable and it closes when people click elsewhere.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The panel is a non-modal `dialog`, named by `title` and described by
  `description`. Without a title, give it an `aria-label`.
- Opening moves focus into the panel; Escape, the close button or a click outside
  closes it and returns focus to the trigger.
- The panel is portalled so it is never clipped. While it is open, `Tab` stays
  within the panel and the rest of the page is hidden from assistive
  technology, so close it to move on.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use a Popover for essential steps.** It closes when people click away.
- **Don't open a Popover on hover.** Use a `Tooltip` for hover hints.
- **Don't put a long form in a Popover.** It scrolls in a small box; use a `Drawer`.

components.title: Presentation
components.purpose: `Presentation` is a render-less context provider that sets the visual **register** (`compact` | `default` | `large` | `hero`) for every register-aware descendant — `Heading`, `Text`, `Button`, `Badge`, `Spinner`, `Avatar`, `TextField`, `Card`, `Section`, and more. It produces no DOM of its own; it only threads a value through context.

guidance.Accessibility:
- `Presentation` has no DOM output and no interactive behavior — it carries no accessibility implications of its own.
- Register changes are purely visual (spacing, type size, control size); they never change semantic markup (heading levels, ARIA roles) on the components inside.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
