- **Don't reach for `Presentation` when a `Section` would already provide the register.** If the content is a top-level page section, use `Section register="…"` — it gives you the register plus the padding/tone chrome in one component.
- **Don't use `Presentation` to set an individual component's size.** If only one `Button` needs to be bigger, that's a sign the library is missing a targeted prop, not a signal to wrap a single component in its own `Presentation`. File it as a component gap rather than working around it.
- **Don't nest more than two or three registers deep.** Each level of nesting makes it harder to predict the effective register at a glance — prefer a flatter structure where each section or card sets its register once.

components.title: Printable, NotPrintable and PrintOnly
components.purpose: Three marks that decide what goes on paper. None of them adds a box or changes anything on screen. Print the example above (Ctrl+P or ⌘P) to see them work: only the statement prints, the app bar and help line are left off, and a letterhead and reference appear.
documentationSections: What every component does on paper

guidance.Accessibility:
`PrintOnly` is hidden on screen from everyone, including screen reader users, so
put nothing there that people on screen need. `NotPrintable` and `Printable`
change nothing on screen.
guidance.Pitfalls:
- **Don't hide what a printed record needs.** A printed statement still needs
  its totals, dates and reference, even when they sit in a part of the screen
  you'd otherwise leave off.
- **Wrap whole regions.** Marking the content you want, once, is sturdier than
  marking everything else `NotPrintable`.
- **A `PrintOnly` outside every `Printable` doesn't print** while a `Printable`
  is on the page, like anything else outside one.

components.title: ProgressBar
components.purpose: `ProgressBar` reports progress on a known-length operation — file upload, multi-step job, batch import. Omit `value` and the bar switches to an indeterminate sliding animation for work whose duration can't be measured. For a fast, one-shot action where there's no spatial layout to reserve, prefer `Spinner`; for placeholders during page load, prefer `Skeleton`.
documentationSections: A theme's own colours as tones

guidance.Accessibility:
- Uses `role="progressbar"` with `aria-valuemin={0}`, `aria-valuemax={100}`, and `aria-valuenow` (determinate only — omitted when indeterminate).
- Provide either a visible `label` or `ariaLabel`; without one, the bar has no name for assistive tech.
- The indeterminate animation slows under `prefers-reduced-motion` from 1.4s to 3s rather than disappearing entirely — the user still sees something is happening.
- Tones are color *and* (when paired with a label) text — never use color alone to convey "error" or "warning".
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't fake progress.** If you don't know how long it'll take, render the indeterminate variant. Slowly counting up to 99% then stalling is worse than no number at all.
- **Don't leave a determinate bar at the same value for >2 seconds.** If it stops moving, swap to indeterminate or surface an error — a frozen number reads as "broken".
- **Don't omit the label.** Screen readers need either `label` or `ariaLabel`. A nameless progress bar is a soundless signal.
- **Don't reuse `tone="error"` for "loading is slow".** Reserve `error` for actual failure states; warnings or a label change ("Retrying…") are better for slowness.

components.title: QrCode
components.purpose: `QrCode` encodes any string — URL, plain text, payload — as a scannable QR image. The SVG fills the square footprint of its parent so layout decisions stay with the consumer; pair it with an optional clickable label that doubles as a fallback for people who can't or won't scan.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The underlying `<svg>` carries `aria-label="QR code for: <value>"` so
  screen-reader users hear what's encoded.
- When a `label` is provided, it renders as a real `<a>` with the same
  `href` as the encoded value — keyboard- and screen-reader-navigable
  without needing camera scanning.
- Anchor focus ring uses `theme.colors.border.focus` for visible focus.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **No fixed width on the component itself.** Size the parent — the QR
  square always fills 100% of it.
- **Don't drop the quiet zone for printed QRs.** Cameras need ~4 modules
  of background; printing right up to the edge will hurt scan rates.
- **Watch contrast under custom colors.** Aim for ≥4:1 between `fgColor`
  and `bgColor`; pastel-on-pastel combos may look on-brand but fail to
  scan reliably.

components.title: RadioGroup
components.purpose: `RadioGroup` is a controlled, single-select group of radio buttons. The library exports the *group* rather than a standalone `Radio` because a lone radio is almost always a UX bug — radios only make sense among mutually-exclusive choices. For two-or-three short options consider `Switch` (binary) or a segmented `Button` group; for many options, prefer a `Select`.

guidance.Accessibility:
Helper and error text are exposed as descriptions, separate from the visible label. A supplied `aria-describedby` is preserved and combined with the component’s message.

- Renders a real `<fieldset>` + `<legend>` so screen readers announce the group's name before each option.
- Native `<input type="radio">` is preserved (visually hidden), so arrow keys cycle through options and Space selects — no custom keybindings needed.
- `error` sets `aria-invalid="true"` on the fieldset, paired with a visible error message styled in `theme.colors.error`.
- The focus ring is the standard `theme.colors.border.focus`, applied to the visible dot via `:has` + `:focus-visible`.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't ship a single radio.** If there's only one choice, it should be a `Checkbox` (consent) or `Switch` (toggle). A lone radio reads as broken.
- **Don't use `RadioGroup` for many options.** Past ~7 options the user can't scan the list; switch to a `Select`.
- **Don't omit the legend.** The legend is the group's accessible name — without it, each option is announced in isolation.
- **Don't put long-form copy in `helperText`.** It's for a one-line clarification. For paragraphs, build a card-based selector instead.

components.title: Relative time
components.purpose: `RelativeTime` shows a moment as how long ago it was, such as "2 hours ago" or "yesterday". Press it to see the full date and time in a small popover.

guidance.Accessibility: The trigger is a button named by both the words and the full date and time, so a screen reader hears the exact moment without opening the popover. The popover opens on Enter or Space and closes on Escape, and focus returns to the time.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Do not use it for a date something is about.** A due date or a release date needs the date itself.
- **Do not put it where people compare times.** In a table people sort and scan, show dates, so the column lines up.
- **Pass ISO strings with a time zone.** A date and time with no offset is read as local time, so it can be hours out.

components.title: ResizablePanels
components.purpose: `ResizablePanels` splits an area into panels the user can resize: a sidebar beside the content, an editor over a terminal, a list beside its detail. Each `ResizablePanel` sets its own default, smallest and largest size, and a `ResizableHandle` between each pair is what people drag, or focus and move with the keyboard.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Each handle follows the WAI-ARIA window splitter pattern: `role="separator"`,
  focusable, with `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin` and `aria-valuemax` giving the
  size of the panel before it in percent, and `aria-controls` pointing at that
  panel. `aria-orientation` is the line's direction: `vertical` between
  side-by-side panels.
- Name every handle with `label`, saying what it resizes ("Resize sidebar",
  "Resize terminal"). The default, "Resize", is ambiguous when there are two.
- The grab target is 24px across (`components.resizable.hitArea`) even though the
  line is a hairline, meeting the WCAG 2.5.8 target size. It overhangs the
  panels' edges, so keep interactive content a few pixels in from the edge.
- Keyboard focus draws the line in the focus-ring colour. Pointer focus doesn't.
- Panels are plain `div`s. If a panel is a landmark or region, give it the
  `role` and `aria-label` it needs.
- The hover transition is turned off with reduced motion.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **The group has no height.** It fills its container, and a container with no
  height gives it none. Size the container, or make it a stretching flex child.
- **Long content pushes nothing, it's clipped.** Panels use `overflow: hidden`
  so their content can't fight the layout while it's resized. Put a scrolling
  region (`ScrollBox`, or a child with `overflow: auto` and `block-size: 100%`)
  inside a panel with long content.
- **Padding on the panel itself.** Panel sizes are shares of the space after
  handles; padding on the panel adds to that. Pad a child instead.
- **Wrapping panels or handles.** Panels and handles must be direct children of
  their `ResizablePanels` (fragments are fine), so the group finds them in order.
- **Pixel defaults on the server.** Pixel sizes need the group's measured size,
  so with server rendering a panel sized in pixels settles after hydration. Use
  percentages for defaults when the first paint matters.
- **Iframes in panels.** While a handle is dragged the group stops panels from
  taking pointer events, so an embedded frame doesn't swallow the drag.

components.title: ScatterChart
components.purpose: `ScatterChart` plots the relationship between two measures, one dot per item: days overdue against the dues owing, tear volume recorded against sightings logged. Use it to spot correlation, clusters and outliers across many items. It is not for change over time (use a [LineChart](?path=/docs/functional-line-chart--docs)) or for comparing totals across categories (use a [BarChart](?path=/docs/functional-bar-chart--docs)). Every point has two numeric values; if one of them is a category, it's a bar chart.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The chart is a `<figure>` named by `title` and described by `description`. `title` is required; `hideTitle` hides it visually only.
- The "Table view" toggle button (`aria-pressed`) swaps the plot for a table with one row per point: its group (when there are several), its name (with `nameKey`) and both values under the axis labels. It is the dependable way to read exact values with a keyboard, screen reader or magnifier.
- The plot is focusable (`role="application"`) and arrow keys move the tooltip between points.
- Colour never works alone: two or more groups get a legend, the tooltip names the point and its values, and the table names each group. Light-mode slots 3 to 5 are under 3:1 contrast on white, which is why the legend and table view are always present.
- Axis titles and tick labels stay in text colours, never a group's colour.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Too many groups.** Past three, colours blur together where points overlap. Use small multiples.
- **Plotting time on the x axis.** Dots over dates hide the sequence. Use a LineChart.
- **Missing or vague axis labels.** "Value" on both axes makes the chart unreadable. Say what each axis measures and give it a unit with `formatX` and `formatY`.
- **No `nameKey` on data about named items.** An outlier nobody can identify starts a hunt through the table. Name the points.
- **Two value axes.** There is one y axis. Different units belong in different charts.
- **Reading correlation as cause.** The chart shows that two measures move together; say in the text what you know about why, or don't claim it.
- **Colouring text to match a group.** Text in slots 3 to 5 fails contrast; let the legend carry the colour.

components.title: ScrollBox
components.purpose: `ScrollBox` is a scrollable wrapper — sets `overflow` along the chosen axis and caps the box at `maxHeight` / `maxWidth`. Use it for long lists in a fixed panel, code blocks that exceed their row, table viewports, or any container whose content can exceed its visible bounds. The opposite-axis overflow is hidden by default (vertical scrolling clips horizontal overflow, and vice-versa); pass `axis="both"` when both axes should scroll independently.
documentationSections: Long list in a fixed panel

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain `<div>` — semantics live in the child.
- Scrollable regions need to be focusable so keyboard users can scroll them. Add `tabIndex={0}` (and an `aria-label` describing the region) when the contained content isn't itself focusable.
- A scroll region nested inside another scroll region is confusing for screen-reader users; keep page-level scroll on `Page` and use ScrollBox sparingly for genuinely separate scroll surfaces.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Vertical scrolling needs a constrained height.** Either pass `maxHeight` here or ensure the parent has a fixed height. Without it, the box grows to fit its content and never scrolls.
- **Don't nest ScrollBox inside another scrolling container** unless you really want two independent scroll regions — most of the time it's a sign the inner one should be removed.
- **For "fade out at the edges" effects**, layer a CSS mask on the parent rather than baking it into ScrollBox. Keeps the scroller composable.
- **Don't put `axis="horizontal"` on a region that should wrap.** If long text inside a ScrollBox forces a horizontal scrollbar, the user probably wanted line wrapping — drop the ScrollBox or constrain width on the child.

components.title: Section
components.purpose: `Section` is the standard marketing/page section: a semantic `<section>` with vertical breathing room (`register`), an optional background `tone`, and an inner `Container` that constrains content to a 1180px shell. Use it to build up a landing or marketing page as a stack of `Section`s — a hero, a features strip, a pricing grid, a footer CTA.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a real `<section>` landmark by default. Pair with a `SectionHeading` and point `aria-labelledby` at the heading's `id` if you need the landmark to have an accessible name for assistive tech that lists landmarks.
- `register` only affects visual scale — it has no accessibility implication of its own; the components inside (Heading levels, focus rings, etc.) carry their own semantics regardless of register.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't nest a `Section` inside another `Section`.** Registers cascade via context, so a nested Section's own `register` prop will win for its subtree, but the double `<section>` landmark and doubled vertical padding rarely reads as intended. Use a plain `Block` or `VStack` for internal grouping instead.
- **Don't fight the `Container` width with your own `maxWidth`.** If content needs to be narrower or wider than 1180px, wrap it in a `Block maxWidth="…"` inside the Section rather than reaching for `BleedSection` and re-adding your own container.
- **Don't use `tone="subtle"` for more than one or two sections per page.** It's a strong visual break — overusing it flattens the hierarchy it's meant to create.

components.title: SectionHeading
components.purpose: `SectionHeading` is the eyebrow + headline + sub-copy block that opens a `Section` — the recurring "small label, big statement, one line of support copy" shape used across marketing and dashboard pages alike.

guidance.Accessibility:
- `SectionHeading` renders the headline as a real `Heading` element (`h1`–`h3` per `level`) — don't wrap it in an additional heading of your own.
- Because `level` is independent of visual size, you can keep a correct, linear heading outline (`h1` → `h2` → `h3`) across a page even as the *visual* weight varies by register.
- The `eyebrow` renders as a `Badge`, which is not itself a heading — screen-reader users navigating by heading will land on the headline, not the eyebrow. Don't put essential information only in the eyebrow.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use `SectionHeading` for body copy.** It's an opening block, not a general two-line paragraph component — for supporting prose elsewhere in a section, use `Text` directly.
- **Don't set `level` based on how big you want the text.** Size comes from the ambient `Presentation` register (usually set by the parent `Section`); `level` is purely semantic. Wrap in `<Presentation register="hero">` if you need to bump the visual size without changing the section it lives in.
- **Don't override `maxWidth` to make the sub-copy wrap awkwardly narrow or wide.** The 720px default is tuned for readability — only override for genuinely different content shapes.

components.title: Select
components.purpose: `Select` is the canonical one-of-many picker: a button that opens a styled listbox, built on React Aria's Select. The listbox flips and shifts at the viewport edges, scrolls when long, and supports full keyboard navigation and type-to-search. A hidden native `<select>` carries the value for forms, so `name`, `form` and `required` behave as before; `ref` reaches the visible trigger button.

guidance.Accessibility:
Helper and error text are exposed as descriptions, separate from the visible label. A supplied `aria-describedby` is preserved and combined with the component’s message.

- The label is a real `<label>` associated with the control; clicking it focuses the trigger.
- `error` sets `aria-invalid="true"` on the select; the error text is connected with `aria-describedby` and kept separate from the field’s accessible name.
- The trigger is a button with `aria-haspopup="listbox"` and `aria-expanded`, named by its value and the label, and described by the helper or error text (a searchable Select's input is `role="combobox"`); the list is `role="listbox"` with `role="option"` items and `aria-selected`. `ArrowDown`/`ArrowUp`/`Enter`/`Space` open it, arrows and typing move the highlight (skipping disabled options), `Enter` selects, `Escape` closes, and focus returns to the trigger.
- The focus ring uses `--squonk-colors-border-focus` with a 2px box-shadow halo — visible against light and dark backgrounds.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't make people scroll more than ~20 options.** Past that, they can't scan the list — add `searchable`.
- **Don't omit the `label`.** A bare select without a label is a screen-reader nightmare. If the label is contextually obvious (e.g. inside a labeled column header), pass `aria-label` instead.
- **Don't put validation results in `helperText`.** Use `error` so the control gets `aria-invalid` and the styling switches; helper text is for format hints only.
- **Don't disable a select without explanation.** Pair with a tooltip or helper text so the user knows why it's locked.

components.title: Sidebar
components.purpose: `Sidebar` renders a vertical, fixed-width column with a surface background and a border on its inside edge — the canonical side-nav shape. It's a semantic `<aside>` by default; render as `<nav>` via `as="nav"` when the contents are exclusively navigation. `Sidebar` is a *flex item* — drop it inside a flex row (the `Page` component or any `HStack`) next to a `<main>` element that takes `flex: 1`.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders `<aside>` by default — announced as a complementary landmark by screen readers.
- For nav-only sidebars, render as `<nav>` (`as="nav" aria-label="Primary"`) so it becomes a navigation landmark with a single skip target.
- Sidebar content is scrollable on overflow (the surface itself owns the scroll), keeping the main content area's scroll independent.
- Keyboard: nothing special — focus traversal is whatever the inner links / buttons supply.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't forget the flex parent.** Without `display: flex` on the surrounding container, the sidebar's `flex: 0 0 <width>` does nothing and the layout collapses.
- **`side` only swaps the divider edge.** Where the sidebar appears visually is set by its DOM order — put it before `<main>` for a left rail, after for right.
- **Don't make the sidebar collapse into a hamburger here.** This component is the desktop rail. For a mobile drawer, build a `Drawer` (out of scope for this library) that *uses* `Sidebar` as the desktop fallback.
- **Don't hardcode width inside.** The sidebar's `width` prop already sets its size. Children should fill the available width with `width: 100%`, not match a hardcoded number.
guidance.Width contract: The default 240px width includes padding and the divider. A custom `width` has the same border-box behavior. The sidebar intentionally does not shrink; use a responsive app layout that hides or relocates navigation when the available width cannot accommodate it. Remove any previous padding/border compensation from surrounding layouts.

components.title: Skeleton
components.purpose: `Skeleton` is a content placeholder shown while data is loading. The point is to pre-allocate the shape of the final layout so the page doesn't jump when content arrives. Use it whenever you know what the loaded UI will look like; use `Spinner` instead when there's no spatial layout to reserve, and `ProgressBar` when you have a measurable percentage.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The skeleton itself is `aria-hidden="true"` — there's nothing meaningful to announce.
- Pair with `aria-busy="true"` on the container that's loading, so assistive tech knows to wait.
- The shimmer animation respects `prefers-reduced-motion` and stops entirely under that preference.
- Color contrast isn't a concern (it's decorative), but the placeholder must visually read as "not yet content" — keep it on `background.subtle`, not on a colored surface that could be mistaken for real content.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't size the skeleton differently from the real content.** The whole point is no layout shift; if the real avatar is 40px and the skeleton is 48px, the page jumps on swap.
- **Don't show a skeleton for sub-300ms requests.** A flash of placeholder is worse than waiting. Add a delay before mounting if you know the request is usually fast.
- **Don't skeleton everything.** Pre-allocate the high-level shape, not every nested element. Five lines of text is enough — don't render 47 word-shaped boxes.
- **Don't forget `aria-busy` on the parent.** Skeletons hide themselves from screen readers; without `aria-busy` on the container, the page reads as empty.

components.title: Spacer
components.purpose: `Spacer` consumes leftover space inside a flex parent — typically used to push two groups of siblings to opposite ends of a row. Use `HStack` with `justify="between"` (or the `Split` named composition) when you can; reach for `Spacer` only when the split isn't symmetric or you need it between specific siblings. `size="auto"` grows; any other token sets a fixed dimension and acts as a structural gap (useful in non-flex contexts).

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders `aria-hidden="true"` — it has no semantic content for assistive tech.
- Doesn't affect focus or tab order.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Prefer `HStack justify="between"` (or `Split`) for the symmetric two-group case.** Spacer is for when there are three+ siblings and only one of the gaps should grow.
- **Doesn't work outside a flex parent when `size="auto"`.** Either set a token size or put it inside an `HStack` / `VStack`.
- **Don't sprinkle Spacers between every child.** That's what `gap` is for — Spacer is for *uneven* gaps.
- **Don't use Spacer to add vertical space between sections.** Use the parent `VStack`'s `gap` or pad the section directly.

components.title: Sparkline
components.purpose: `Sparkline` is a word-sized trend line with no axes, gridlines or tooltip. Put it beside a figure or in a table cell to show which way something has been heading: up, down, flat or spiky. It shows shape, not values, so always put the exact figure next to it. When people need to read individual points or compare series, use a [LineChart](?path=/docs/functional-line-chart--docs) instead.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The sparkline is one image (`role="img"`). Screen readers hear its `label` with the first and last values, for example "Sightings logged, last 12 weeks: 120 to 230". Write `label` as what the line shows and over what period.
- Use `formatValue` so those values are read with their unit ("$4,200 to $1,500"), not as bare numbers.
- It isn't focusable and has no tooltip, so nothing in it is only reachable by mouse. Anything people must read exactly belongs in the text next to it.
- Colour carries no meaning here: a falling line is drawn in the same colour as a rising one. If falling is bad news, say so in words, or use a Stat with `increaseIs`.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Sparkline on its own.** Without a figure or label next to it, people can see a shape but not what it means or where it ended. Pair it with the number.
- **Comparing sizes between sparklines.** Each is scaled to its own range, so a line that fills its box may be far smaller than one that barely moves. Use a [BarChart](?path=/docs/functional-bar-chart--docs) or a LineChart with shared axes to compare amounts.
- **A vague `label`.** "Trend" tells a screen reader user nothing. Say the measure and the period.
- **Painting it red or green to mean good or bad.** Status colours are for text and icons that say good or bad in words; keep the sparkline in a palette slot.
- **Too few points.** Two or three values make a straight line or a single bend; show the numbers instead.

components.title: Spinner
components.purpose: `Spinner` is the busy indicator for short, indeterminate operations — submitting a form, sending a one-shot request, swapping a tab. For *known* progress with a measurable duration, prefer `ProgressBar`; for loading a content area where the final shape is known, prefer `Skeleton`.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders inside `role="status"` with `aria-live="polite"` so screen readers announce the operation without interrupting.
- The visible ring carries `aria-hidden="true"`; the announced text comes from a visually-hidden `<span>` (defaults to "Loading", overridable via `label`).
- Respects `prefers-reduced-motion` by slowing the spin from 800ms to 1800ms — the indicator stays useful without becoming a vestibular trigger.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't show a spinner for a layout area you could skeleton.** If you know the loaded content has shape (a card, a list row), `Skeleton` reduces layout shift; `Spinner` doesn't.
- **Don't pair a spinner with a misleading "X% complete" label.** If you have a percentage, you have known progress — use `ProgressBar`.
- **Don't render multiple spinners side-by-side.** They visually compete; one parent-level spinner usually serves better.
- **Don't spin forever.** If the underlying request can hang, set a timeout in the consuming code and swap to an error state — a perpetual spinner is the worst kind of frozen UI.

components.title: Split
components.purpose: `Split` is a horizontal row whose children are pushed to opposite ends — the canonical "leading group | trailing group" pattern: a title with a trailing action, a card header with a status badge, a list-item with a value on the right. Reach for `Split` whenever the *intent* is "these things are at opposite ends of the row". For a wrapping flow of items, use `Cluster`; for a strict row with a custom layout, use `HStack` directly.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain `<div>` row — semantics come from what you put inside.
- The visual "opposite ends" arrangement is purely flex-driven; DOM order is preserved, so screen readers and keyboard users see the leading group first.
- For headings + actions, give the action a verb-led label (`New session`, not just `New`) so screen-reader users get the same context sighted users get from proximity.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use Split for more than two groups.** It's two-ended — third items end up jammed in the middle. For 3+ groups, use `HStack` with explicit `justify="between"` and group children.
- **Don't shove a long string straight into Split.** Without a max-width or `min-width: 0`, a long unbreakable string blows the row out. Wrap text in a parent that constrains it.
- **Don't enable `wrap` by default.** Splits visually communicate "these are paired at opposite ends" — wrapping breaks that intent. Enable it only when you've actually got narrow-screen breakage.
- **Don't reach for Split when nothing should split.** A row of evenly-spaced items is a `Cluster`, not a Split with `justify="between"`.

components.title: Stat
components.purpose: `Stat` shows one headline figure with its label, and optionally how it changed against an earlier period and a sparkline of recent values. Sometimes the right chart is a number: when people need to know "how many" or "how much" right now, a Stat says it faster than any plot. It has no surface of its own, so place it in a [Card](?path=/docs/layout-card--docs), or a [Grid](?path=/docs/layout-primitives-grid--docs) of Cards for a row of figures. It doesn't format the figure for you or fetch anything.
documentationSections: Good news, bad news or neither

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a description list: the label is the `<dt>`, the figure, change and trend are its `<dd>`s, so screen readers announce them as one term with its details.
- Direction is never colour alone. The change shows an arrow and a sign, and screen readers hear "Up" or "Down" before the percentage ("Up +12.4% vs last month"). The green and red come from the status text tokens, which meet text contrast in light and dark modes.
- The trend sparkline is an image named by `trendLabel` with its first and last values. Leave `trendLabel` at its default ("Trend") and that name says nothing.
- Stat isn't interactive. If the figure links to a detail page, put a link in the Card, or use an InteractiveCard; don't wrap the Stat in a button.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **A change without `changeLabel`.** "+8%" against what? Always say the comparison period.
- **Leaving `increaseIs` at `good` for a bad measure.** A rise in overdue dues shown in green tells people the opposite of the truth. Decide for every Stat.
- **Passing a percentage to `change`.** `change={12.4}` reads "+1,240%". Pass the fraction, `0.124`.
- **Unformatted or over-precise figures.** `value={86634.37}` is hard to read at a glance. Format and round it ("$86.6K"), and give the exact figure in a table or detail view.
- **A Stat floating on the page.** It has no surface or padding of its own; put it in a Card.
- **Too many figures in a row.** Past four, nothing stands out. Lead with the figures people act on and move the rest into a table.

components.title: Switch
components.purpose: `Switch` is a binary toggle for settings that take effect *immediately* — flipping it sends the change right now. Visually distinct from `Checkbox` (which stages a value to be submitted later) on purpose. Use `Switch` for preferences and live toggles; use `Checkbox` for form fields and multi-select.

guidance.Accessibility:
Helper and error text are exposed as descriptions, separate from the visible label. A supplied `aria-describedby` is preserved and combined with the component’s message.

- Uses a real `<input type="checkbox">` with `role="switch"` — assistive tech announces the control as a toggle (not as a generic checkbox).
- Keyboard: Space toggles the state; Tab moves focus. Enter does not toggle a native checkbox.
- The focus ring lives on the visible track and shows for keyboard focus only, using `--squonk-colors-border-focus`.
- The wrapping `<label>` makes the whole row clickable, including helper text — no `htmlFor` plumbing needed.
- An uncontrolled switch returns to `defaultChecked` when its form resets, and a disabled ancestor `<fieldset>` disables it.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use a Switch in a form that submits.** Switches imply immediate effect. If the user has to click "Save" for the change to take hold, use a `Checkbox` instead.
- **Don't ship a switch with destructive immediate effect and no confirmation.** "Delete on shutdown" should not be a one-click toggle — add a confirmation step.
- **Don't disable a switch without explanation.** A non-interactive toggle is confusing; pair `disabled` with helper text explaining why.
- **Don't forget to forward `onChange`.** The first argument is the new boolean — not the event. Read the signature before swapping in a native input handler.

components.title: Table
components.purpose: `Table` renders typed column definitions over an array of rows — the workhorse for admin lists, reports, and any grid of records. The outermost element is a horizontally-scrolling wrapper, so a wide table scrolls inside its container instead of stretching the page.
documentationSections: Migration: typed columns and stable rows

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a real `<table>` with `<thead>` / `<th scope="col">` semantics, so
  screen readers announce column context per cell.
- `caption` renders a visually-hidden `<caption>` naming the table — set it
  whenever the surrounding page doesn't already title the data.
- A visually hidden live region announces the row count after filtering and,
  in a reading table, sort changes ("Sorted by Age, descending"). In a grid,
  React Aria announces sort and selection changes itself.
- In a reading table with `pageSize`, the table sets `aria-rowcount` to the
  full filtered count and each row its `aria-rowindex`, so position is
  announced across pages.
- As an interactive grid (`role="grid"`, React Aria's `Table`), the grid is a
  single tab stop, so `Tab` moves past it. Focus starts on a row; `↑`/`↓`
  move between rows, `←`/`→` move into and between the row's cells and up to
  the column headers, `Home`/`End` and `Ctrl+Home`/`Ctrl+End` jump, `Space`
  selects the row, and `Enter` on a sortable column header sorts it. Selected
  rows carry `aria-selected`. If the focused row is filtered out or deleted,
  focus moves to a remaining row. On Android, React Aria describes the sort
  order instead of setting `aria-sort`, which TalkBack ignores.
guidance.Pitfalls:
- Keys in `rows` objects are looked up by `column.key` only when `render` is
  absent; non-primitive values should always go through `render`.
- Provide `rowKey` whenever rows can reorder — the index fallback breaks
  React reconciliation for dynamic data.
guidance.Reading and responsive contract:
By default this is a semantic reading table, not an ARIA grid: embedded links and buttons stay in the normal tab sequence. Opt into the grid only when rows are selectable or cells hold controls that would otherwise make Tab tedious; see the [WAI table](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/table/) and [grid](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/) patterns, and the [Tables and grids](?path=/docs/patterns-tables-and-grids--docs) guidance.

At narrow widths, preserve header-to-cell relationships and allow the existing wrapper to scroll. Check that keyboard users can reach overflowing content, and place filters or pagination outside that horizontal scroller. Compose [Skeleton](?path=/docs/functional-skeleton--docs) for loading, [Alert](?path=/docs/functional-alert--docs) for load failure, and [EmptyState](?path=/docs/layout-empty-state--docs) for a successful query with no records; an empty `rows` array cannot distinguish these states itself.

components.title: Tabs
components.purpose: `Tabs` switch between related panels in the same place, so people can move between sections of one thing (a membership's overview, sightings and payments) without leaving the page. Only one panel shows at a time.
documentationSections: A tab list that stays in view

guidance.Accessibility:
- The WAI-ARIA tabs pattern: a `tablist` of `tab`s, each controlling a `tabpanel`
  labelled by its tab.
- The list is a single Tab stop. Arrow keys move between tabs, Home and End go to
  the ends, and disabled tabs are skipped. The next Tab press moves into the panel.
- By default a tab is selected as soon as focus reaches it. Use
  `activationMode="manual"` when panels are slow to render, so arrowing past a tab
  doesn't load it.
- Name the list with `listLabel` unless a heading right above already names it.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use tabs for navigation between pages.** Tabs don't change the URL or
  the browser history.
- **Don't hide something people must do inside a tab they might not open.** Put
  required fields where they can be seen.
- **Don't nest tabs inside tabs.**

components.title: Tag
components.purpose: `Tag` is a compact label for a category, keyword, applied filter or entered value. It names something; it can be removed. Use `Badge` for a *status* ("Overdue", "Live", "3 new"), and `Tag` for things people add, choose or filter by.
documentationSections: A theme's own colours as tones

guidance.Accessibility:
- A lone tag is a plain `<span>`; React Aria's TagGroup needs a set of tags,
  so use `TagGroup` for a row of them.
- The remove button is a real `<button>` (a React Aria Button) named "Remove <text>", so a row of
  tags reads as "Remove Night watches", "Remove Overdue". Pass `removeLabel` when the
  content isn't plain text.
- After a tag is removed, its button disappears. When removing from a list, move
  focus to the next tag's remove button or to the list's heading so keyboard
  users aren't dropped at the top of the page.
- Colour is never the only signal: the tag's text says what it is.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use a Tag as a button or link.** A tag isn't interactive apart from its
  remove button. For a choice among options, use a `RadioGroup`, a
  `CheckboxGroup` or a toggle.
- **Don't use a Tag for status.** "Paid" and "Overdue" are `Badge`s.
- **Don't colour every tag differently.** A rainbow of tones reads as noise.

components.title: Text
components.purpose:
`Text` is the body-copy primitive — every paragraph, label, caption, or inline string that isn't a heading or input. Renders a `

` by default; use `as="span"` for inline use. Size tracks the surrounding `Presentation` register, so a `Text` in a `compact` panel and one in a `hero` section both feel right without a `size` prop.

guidance.Accessibility:
- The default `

` is the semantically correct container for a paragraph; `as="span"` for inline runs preserves the surrounding flow. - Tone is paired with the text content — never use color alone to convey error or success. - An eyebrow is uppercased with CSS, so screen readers get the text as you wrote it. Write it in sentence case, not capitals. - Truncation hides text visually but it remains accessible to screen readers (the full string is still in the DOM); consider adding a `title` for sighted hover discoverability. - Contrast for every tone is verified against the theme backgrounds in `theme.colors.text.*` — both light and dark themes meet WCAG AA.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use an eyebrow as a heading.** It has no heading role, and capitals are slow to read: keep it to a few words above a real `Heading`.
- **Don't reach for a `size` prop — there isn't one.** Wrap in a `Presentation` register; that way other nested primitives scale together.
- **Don't pile up `tone="error"` for non-error content.** Save the red for things the user must address. For ordinary "couldn't load" hints, use `secondary` or `muted`.
- **Don't use `Text as="span"` and forget surrounding line-height.** Inline text inherits the parent's line-height; an inline `Text` inside a tightly-spaced container can read awkwardly. Wrap the parent in a regular paragraph if needed.
- **Don't truncate without constraining the parent.** `truncate` needs a bounded width to clip against. Inside a flex child, add `min-width: 0` so the child can shrink past its content.

components.title: TextField
components.purpose: `TextField` is the canonical single-line text input — email, password, URL, search, anything that fits on one row. The `<label>` is associated with the input, so clicking it focuses the field; `error` switches the input into a validated state with `aria-invalid` set. For multi-line text use a `Textarea`; for one-of-many use `Select` or `RadioGroup`.

guidance.Accessibility:
Helper and error text are exposed as descriptions, separate from the visible label. A supplied `aria-describedby` is preserved and combined with the component’s message.

- The label is a real `<label>` associated with the input by `for`/`id` (pass `id` to choose it), so a label click focuses the input. `required`, `disabled` and `readOnly` reach the input, and an error message is announced politely when it appears.
- `error` sets `aria-invalid="true"` on the input; the error text is connected with `aria-describedby` and kept separate from the field’s accessible name.
- The focus ring uses `--squonk-colors-border-focus` with a 2px box-shadow halo — visible against light and dark backgrounds.
- All standard `<input>` props (`autoComplete`, `inputMode`, `pattern`, `required`) are forwarded — accessibility hints work as expected.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't use the placeholder as a label.** Placeholders disappear on focus and are low-contrast — always pair them with a real `label`.
- **Don't put validation results in `helperText`.** Use `error` so the field gets `aria-invalid` and the styling switches; helper text is for format hints only.
- **Don't forget `type` for non-text fields.** `type="email"` triggers the right mobile keyboard and gives free browser validation; `type="password"` masks the value.
- **Don't disable a field without explanation.** Pair with a tooltip or helper text so the user knows why it's locked.
guidance.Validation and submission ownership: `TextField` renders the supplied error; it does not validate data, decide when an error appears, submit requests or focus the first invalid field. Keep entered values when submission fails, explain how to correct each invalid value, and connect a form-level error summary to the affected fields when several errors occur. Use persistent [Alert](?path=/docs/functional-alert--docs) feedback for a failed save; a disappearing toast should not be the only recovery instruction. See [WAI form notifications](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/notifications/).

components.title: Textarea
components.purpose: `Textarea` takes several lines of free text: a reason, a description, a message. It has the same label, helper and error behaviour as `TextField`, so the two sit together in a form. Use `TextField` for anything that fits on one line (names, numbers, references).
documentationSections: Size it to the expected answer

guidance.Accessibility:
- The label is associated by `for`/`id`; helper, error and count text are
  descriptions. A supplied `aria-describedby` is kept and combined with them.
- `error` sets `aria-invalid` and is announced politely when it appears.
- Avoid a placeholder as the only instruction: it disappears when people start
  typing. Put guidance in `helperText`.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't set a `maxLength` you haven't explained.** If there is a limit, show
  it with `showCount` so people aren't cut off mid-sentence.
- **Don't use `autoResize` in a fixed-height layout,** such as a dialog without
  scrolling. The box can push the actions off screen.

components.title: ThemeModifier
components.purpose: `ThemeModifier` scopes a **partial theme override** to a subtree — pass any subset of the theme shape and every `@squonk/ui` component underneath that reads the overridden keys picks up the new values. Outside the wrapped subtree, the theme is unchanged.

guidance.Accessibility:
- `ThemeModifier` changes color values only — it does not itself vet the result for contrast. If you override `colors.primary` (or any text/background pairing), re-check contrast against WCAG AA in both light and dark mode; the library can't verify an arbitrary override for you.
- No DOM output, no interactive behavior, no ARIA implications of its own.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't hand-pick a color without checking contrast in dark mode too.** `ThemeModifier` overrides the value directly — it bypasses the built-in `getMinContrastTextColor` safeguards some components (like `Card`'s `featured` variant) otherwise apply automatically.
- **Don't use `ThemeModifier` for spacing/font/radius scaling.** That's `ThemeStyleBlock`'s job (`register`) — it derives cleanly from primitives and won't compound when nested, whereas stacking `ThemeModifier` size overrides would.
- **Don't wrap the entire app in a `ThemeModifier` for the base theme.** That's what `SquonkThemeProvider` (with `primitives`) is for — `ThemeModifier` is for a *subtree* override layered on top of an already-provided theme.

components.title: ThemeStyleBlock
components.purpose: One style component that retunes the active theme for a subtree on two orthogonal axes:

guidance.Composition and scaling contract:
Primitive changes are rebuilt first, then inherited resolved modifiers and semantic surface boundaries are reapplied in nesting order. This preserves brand overrides and readable text inside an already-painted Card or Alert. An explicit resolved token override wins over the derived value. `register="normal"` restores root-derived sizing, while preserving those explicit overrides.

Spacing-driven layout gaps, card/header/section padding, theme-based body text and Heading sizes scale from their primitives. The layout/heading register values are exposed under `theme.presentation`. Unitless line heights, em tracking, fluid viewport slopes and intentionally fixed control geometry retain their component-specific behavior. See the Theme page's scalability table for the boundaries; this is not a uniform CSS zoom of every pixel.
guidance.Accessibility and responsive checks:
This provider adds no DOM landmark, label, focus behavior or breakpoint. Keep those responsibilities on its child components and page layout. A compact register changes some dimensions; it does not establish that every control still has an adequate pointer target or readable text. Check the smallest register with keyboard focus, long translated labels, browser zoom and a narrow viewport.

An inverted subtree needs a matching painted surface, such as `Block background="default"`; changing context alone does not paint the background. Verify text, borders and focus indicators against that actual surface. Prefer [Presentation](?path=/docs/style-presentation--docs) for a component's supported density register and [ThemeModifier](?path=/docs/style-theme-modifier--docs) for a deliberately scoped token override.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- Do not use a compact register to hide content that fails to fit. Let [Grid](?path=/docs/layout-primitive-grid--docs) or wrapping stacks reorganize the layout.
- Do not compensate for nested registers with arbitrary pixel overrides. Root-derived scaling and explicit semantic overrides have different responsibilities.

components.title: Toast
components.purpose: Transient notifications that stack in a viewport corner and auto-dismiss. `ToastProvider` renders the stack (portal on `document.body`) and publishes the imperative `useToast` handle. Toasts render as elevated `Alert`s, so tones and dark mode follow the ambient theme.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Each notification uses Alert’s status/alert semantics. The surrounding Notifications region does not add a second, nested live region.
- `F6` or `Alt+T` moves focus to the Notifications region, and `Escape` dismisses the focused toast. When a focused toast closes, focus moves to the next toast, or back to where it was before.
- Error and warning toasts render `Alert`'s `role="alert"`, which announces
  assertively.
- Every toast gets a Dismiss button; auto-dismiss never removes the user's
  only chance to act — put required actions on the page, not in a toast.
- An `action` is a real `<button>` inside the toast's Alert, after the message
  and before Dismiss in the tab order. It is read out with the message
  ("Case archived. Undo, button"), and the timer pauses while the toast is
  hovered or focused. People who miss the toast still need the same action on
  the page.
guidance.Pitfalls:
- `useToast` throws outside a `ToastProvider` — mount the provider above
  anything that fires toasts (including error boundaries that report).
- Don't use toasts for validation errors next to a form field; that's
  `TextField`'s `error` prop.

components.title: Tooltip
components.purpose: `Tooltip` shows a short hint when someone hovers or tabs to a control. It is for *extra* information: naming an icon-only button, or explaining a term. Anything a person needs in order to finish the task belongs on the page, because touch screens have no hover and many people never discover a tooltip.

guidance.Accessibility:
- While open, the trigger's `aria-describedby` points at the hint, so screen
  readers announce it after the control's name. It is a description, not a name:
  an icon-only control still needs its own `aria-label`.
- Opens on keyboard focus as well as hover. `Escape` closes it without moving focus.
- The pointer can move onto the hint without it closing, and it stays until the
  pointer or focus leaves (WCAG 1.4.13, content on hover or focus).
- The hint has `role="tooltip"` and must not contain links, buttons or other
  controls. Use a `Popover` for interactive content.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't wrap a disabled button.** Disabled buttons fire no pointer or focus
  events, so the tooltip never opens. Explain why something is unavailable in
  helper text instead.
- **Don't put essential instructions in a tooltip.** Touch users can't hover;
  show the information on the page.
- **Don't wrap plain text.** The trigger must be focusable, or keyboard users
  can't reach the hint.
- **Don't repeat the visible label.** "Save" on a button labelled "Save" adds
  noise for screen-reader users.

components.title: VStack
components.purpose: `VStack` arranges its children vertically (top to bottom) with a token-driven gap and sensible alignment props. It is **not** a styled container — no padding, border, or background, only arrangement. For horizontal arrangement use `HStack`; for two-dimensional layouts use `Grid`.

guidance.Accessibility:
- Renders a plain `<div>` — no roles, no announcements. Children supply their own semantics.
- DOM order is reading order; flex `justify` doesn't change traversal.
- For a list of equivalent items, render as `<ul>` (`as="ul"`) and wrap children in `<li>` so screen readers announce the count.
guidance.Common pitfalls:
- **Don't add margins to children.** The whole point of VStack is that the parent owns the spacing. If you find yourself reaching for `margin-top` on a child, change the `gap` instead.
- **`align="stretch"` is the default.** Children fill the cross-axis (full width). Switch to `align="start"` if you want them to size to their content.
- **Need horizontal arrangement?** Use `HStack` — they are peer components, not variants of one another.
- **Don't reach for VStack for a single centered child.** `Centered` exists for exactly that — using a VStack with `align="center" justify="center"` and `minHeight` is the long way around.
